Module: Food Toxicology, Inherent Plant and Animal Toxicants, Contaminants, Residues and Heavy Metals

This handout is written as a Senior Professor and Chief Paper Setter would teach: molecule first, then clinical pathology, then analytical identification, then the statutory ceiling, then the answer skeleton. Every section is complete; nothing is left as a placeholder.

2. Examination architecture (HPSC pattern)
Stage 1: Objective Screening Test
100 marks, multiple-choice, penalty of 0.25 mark per wrong answer.

Favourite formats: count-based pair questions (Only 1 / Only 2 / All 3 / None), assertion-reason, match-the-following, and absolute-qualifier statements using words such as always, only, never, all, completely.

Expected score of answering a question with probability p of being right: E = 1.25p minus 0.25. Answering is mathematically favourable when p is greater than 0.20, that is, when you can eliminate at least one of four options with confidence.
Stage 2: Subject Knowledge Test
150 marks, 3 hours, conventional descriptive answers, carrying 87.5 percent weightage in final merit.
Time budget: 1.2 minutes per mark. A 10-mark answer gets about 12 minutes; a 15-mark answer about 18 minutes. Reserve 10 to 15 minutes for planning and review.

Scoring architecture for a toxicology answer: Definition, Source and chemistry, Mechanism (with a labelled pathway), Clinical pathology, Analytical identification, Statutory position, Processing or control, Conclusion.
Stage 1 method for count-based pairs
Treat each pair as an independent True or False item.
Underline the subject, the predicate and the qualifier.
Assign c = 1 for a correct pair and c = 0 for a wrong pair.
Compute N = c1 + c2 + c3 and map N to the option.
Never let the familiarity of the topic decide the answer; the predicate decides.

Part 1A: Legume Toxicants
PART 1A: LEGUME TOXICANTS AND ANTINUTRITIONAL FACTORS
First-principles orientation

Legumes are seeds. A seed must survive insects, fungi and predators until germination, so it stores chemical defences: neurotoxic amino acids, cyanide-releasing glycosides, pro-oxidant glycosides, carbohydrate-binding proteins, protease inhibitors and phosphorus locked as phytate. Human processing (soaking, germination, fermentation, moist heat) is essentially a set of counter-strategies against these defences. Every toxicant below is best understood by asking three questions: what is the molecule, what does it hit in the human body, and which processing step breaks it.
1. Lathyrism and Khesari Dal (Lathyrus sativus)
1.1 Botany and epidemiology

Lathyrus sativus is called khesari, kesari dal, teora, chickling vetch or grass pea. It is drought-hardy and cheap, so it dominates the diet of the poorest cultivators in Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Odisha and Maharashtra in drought years.

Neurolathyrism appears when khesari supplies more than about 30 percent of dietary energy for 2 to 6 months, typically in young adult males aged 15 to 45, often during famine when it is eaten unprocessed as roasted seeds or coarse flour.
Historical context: Sleeman (1844) described it in Central India; the Lathyrism Enquiry Field Unit of the Indian Council of Medical Research worked at Rewa in the 1950s and 1960s.
1.2 The molecule
Toxin: beta-N-oxalyl-L-alpha,beta-diaminopropionic acid, abbreviated BOAA, also called ODAP (3-N-oxalyl-L-2,3-diaminopropanoic acid).

Structure: a non-protein amino acid in which the beta-amino group of L-2,3-diaminopropionic acid is acylated by oxalic acid. Two isomers exist: beta-ODAP (the neurotoxic form, about 95 percent of the total) and alpha-ODAP (far less toxic); heating can interconvert them.
Content: 0.1 to 2.5 percent of seed dry weight depending on variety and drought stress. Low-toxin lines (ODAP below 0.1 percent) such as Pusa 24 and Ratan have been bred.
It is water-soluble, which is the entire basis of the detoxification chemistry.
1.3 Mechanism of neurotoxicity

BOAA / ODAP (structural analogue of glutamate)
        |
        v
Agonist at AMPA-type ionotropic glutamate receptors on motor neurons
        |
        v
Sustained sodium and calcium influx (excitotoxicity)
        |
        v
Mitochondrial complex I inhibition, reactive oxygen species,
glutathione depletion, inhibition of glutamate uptake by astrocytes
        |
        v
Selective degeneration of Betz cells and the lateral corticospinal
(pyramidal) tracts supplying the lower limbs
        |
        v
Irreversible spastic paraparesis
Why lower limbs: the longest corticospinal axons, those to the legs, are most vulnerable to energy failure.
Synergistic risk factors: low intake of sulphur amino acids (methionine and cysteine deplete glutathione), zinc deficiency, hard physical labour, and febrile illness.
1.4 Clinical pathology

rows: Calf cramps, heaviness of legs, nocturnal spasms after a heavy khesari meal
Needs one stick; scissoring gait, crossed adductor spasm, toe-walking
Cannot stand; moves on all fours

blocks.text: Upper motor neuron signs: hypertonia, exaggerated knee and ankle jerks, ankle clonus, extensor plantar response (Babinski sign). Sensation, bladder and intellect are usually spared.
The lesion is irreversible; there is no antidote. Prevention is entirely dietary and regulatory.
1.5 Processing detoxification (all exploit water solubility)

rows: Soak dehusked dal in 2 to 3 volumes of water at 60 to 70 degrees Celsius for 1 hour, discard water, wash
Soak overnight, steam or boil in excess water for 15 to 20 minutes, discard water, sun-dry
Soak in 1 to 2 percent calcium hydroxide (lime water) for several hours, wash; alkaline pH hydrolyses the oxalyl amide bond
Lactic fermentation (as in idli or dhokla batter)
Little or no removal; dry heat does not remove a water-soluble toxin

blocks.text: The examiner's favourite pairing: the method must be a wet method with discarding of the soak water. Any question stating that roasting detoxifies khesari is false.
1.6 Statutory position
The Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules (Rule 44A, 1961) prohibited the sale of khesari gram and its products in any form.

This continues under the Food Safety and Standards (Prohibition and Restrictions on Sales) Regulations, 2011, which prohibit the sale of kesari gram (Lathyrus sativus), kesari dal, kesari flour and any admixture of kesari with other grams, dal or flour.

In 2016 the FSSAI scientific panel reviewed lifting the ban in view of low-toxin varieties, but the sale prohibition remains the examinable legal position; a notification lifting it has not been finalised.

Analytical detection in adulterated dal: khesari dal is wedge-shaped with a square truncated end, unlike the rounder lentil or red gram; the chemical test is the 50 percent hydrochloric acid test (pink colour on heating with the dal in dilute hydrochloric acid indicates khesari).

[HPSC EXAM TRAP] Neurolathyrism (from Lathyrus sativus, BOAA) must not be confused with osteolathyrism (from Lathyrus odoratus, sweet pea, caused by beta-aminopropionitrile, which inhibits lysyl oxidase and weakens collagen). A pair that assigns BOAA to skeletal deformity is false.
2. Cyanogenic Glycosides
2.1 The molecules and their sources

rows: Bitter almonds, apricot, peach, plum and cherry kernels, apple seeds
Intermediate in amygdalin breakdown; wild cherry

blocks.text: The intact glycoside is non-toxic. The plant stores it in the vacuole and keeps the hydrolysing enzyme in a separate compartment (cell wall or cytoplasm). Chewing, grating, grinding or insect damage breaks the compartments.
2.2 Enzymatic hydrolysis

Cyanogenic glycoside
        | beta-glucosidase (linamarase in cassava, emulsin in almonds)
        v
Sugar + cyanohydrin (alpha-hydroxynitrile)
        | hydroxynitrile lyase, or spontaneous at pH above 5 and warm temperature
        v
Carbonyl compound (benzaldehyde, acetone) + hydrogen cyanide (HCN)
Gut bacteria also possess beta-glucosidases, so swallowed intact glycoside can still release cyanide in the colon. This is why 'eat it raw without chewing' is not safe.
2.3 Mechanism of cyanide toxicity
Cyanide ion binds the ferric iron (Fe3+) of cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV) in the mitochondrial electron transport chain.
Electron transfer to oxygen stops; oxidative phosphorylation ceases; cells switch to anaerobic glycolysis, producing lactic acidosis.
Result is histotoxic hypoxia: arterial blood stays bright red and oxygen-saturated, but tissues cannot use it. Venous blood is also bright red, a classical sign.

Detoxification in the body: the mitochondrial enzyme rhodanese transfers sulphur from thiosulphate to cyanide, forming the far less toxic thiocyanate, which is excreted in urine. This is why sodium thiosulphate is an antidote and why chronic cassava eaters have high urinary thiocyanate (and secondary goitre, because thiocyanate blocks iodide uptake).
2.4 Clinical pathology

rows: Headache, dizziness, bitter-almond odour, tachypnoea then respiratory depression, convulsions, coma, death within minutes to hours; lethal oral dose of HCN about 0.5 to 3.5 mg/kg body weight (50 to 200 mg in an adult)

Abrupt, permanent, symmetrical spastic paraparesis in cassava-dependent populations of Central and East Africa during drought, linked to inadequately processed bitter cassava plus protein (sulphur amino acid) deficiency
Chronic sensory ataxia, optic atrophy, deafness in long-term low-dose cassava eaters (Nigeria)
Thiocyanate competes with iodide at the thyroid sodium-iodide symporter

blocks.text: Antidotes: hydroxocobalamin (binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin), sodium nitrite (induces methaemoglobin, which scavenges cyanide), sodium thiosulphate (substrate for rhodanese), and 100 percent oxygen.
2.5 Detoxification by processing
Each step either frees the HCN (by letting the enzyme act) or removes it (HCN is volatile, boiling point 26 degrees Celsius, and water-soluble).

rows: Peel of bitter cassava carries most of the linamarin
Ruptures compartments so linamarase meets linamarin
Essential to liberate HCN before heating
Soaking in water (3 to 5 days, retting)
Hydrolysis plus leaching of soluble glycoside and cyanide into water
Slow drying allows enzyme hydrolysis then volatilisation of HCN
Lactic bacteria and endogenous enzymes complete hydrolysis; acid pH keeps cyanohydrin stable so a later heating step is needed
Volatilises HCN and destroys enzyme; must follow grating, because boiling first inactivates the enzyme and locks the glycoside inside

blocks.text: Statutory and Codex ceilings: sweet cassava 50 mg/kg total HCN; cassava flour 10 mg/kg; gari 2 mg/kg. Bitter cassava carries more than 100 mg/kg and up to 1,000 mg/kg fresh weight.

[HPSC EXAM TRAP] Boiling intact chunks of bitter cassava without grating is less effective than grating followed by soaking, because the enzyme that liberates HCN is itself denatured by heat. Sun-drying is only effective if the tissue is first crushed or kept moist long enough for hydrolysis. Also note that amygdalin is wrongly marketed as 'vitamin B17' or laetrile; it has no vitamin status and causes cyanide poisoning.
3. Favism and Faba Beans (Vicia faba)
3.1 The molecules
Vicine and convicine are pyrimidine beta-glucosides concentrated in the cotyledons of faba (broad) beans at 0.5 to 1.0 percent dry weight.
Hydrolysis by beta-glucosidase (in the bean, in gut bacteria and in the intestinal mucosa) removes glucose to give the aglycones divicine (from vicine) and isouramil (from convicine).

Divicine and isouramil are unstable 2,6-diaminopyrimidine-diols that autoxidise rapidly, generating hydrogen peroxide and superoxide radicals and oxidising reduced glutathione (GSH) to oxidised glutathione (GSSG).
3.2 The genetic lesion: G6PD deficiency

Glucose-6-phosphate
        | glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD), first step of the pentose phosphate pathway
        v
6-Phosphogluconolactone + NADPH
        |
        v
NADPH is the only source of reducing power in the mature red cell
        |
        v
Glutathione reductase uses NADPH to regenerate GSH from GSSG
The red blood cell has no mitochondria and no nucleus; the pentose phosphate pathway is its sole NADPH source.

In G6PD deficiency (X-linked, hence mainly affecting males; common in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, African and Indian populations, including Parsis and some tribal groups), NADPH supply fails under oxidant stress.

Divicine and isouramil deplete GSH faster than it can be regenerated; haemoglobin is oxidised to methaemoglobin and denatured into Heinz bodies that precipitate on the membrane; the spleen removes damaged cells (extravascular haemolysis) and some cells lyse in circulation (intravascular haemolysis).
3.3 Clinical pathology

Acute haemolytic anaemia 24 to 48 hours after eating fresh or dried faba beans (or inhaling pollen in sensitive children): pallor, jaundice, dark red-brown urine (haemoglobinuria), fever, back and abdominal pain, tachycardia; severe cases progress to acute kidney injury and death.

Laboratory: fall in haemoglobin, raised unconjugated bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase, reduced haptoglobin, Heinz bodies on supravital stain, 'bite cells' on the smear, reticulocytosis after recovery.

Children aged 1 to 5 years are most affected. The same oxidant mechanism is triggered by primaquine, sulphonamides, naphthalene mothballs and infections, so favism is one member of a wider family of G6PD haemolytic crises.
3.4 Control
Vicine and convicine are heat-stable, so ordinary cooking does not protect a G6PD-deficient person; soaking removes only part because the glycosides are only moderately water-soluble.
Low-vicine faba bean genotypes (vc minus gene) carry less than 10 percent of normal levels.
Dietary avoidance by affected individuals and neonatal G6PD screening are the practical controls.

[HPSC EXAM TRAP] Favism is not an allergy and not a cyanide poisoning. The bean is harmless to people with normal G6PD. A statement that 'faba beans are toxic to all consumers' is false; a statement that 'cooking abolishes favism' is also false.
4. Phytohaemagglutinins (Lectins)
4.1 Nature

Lectins are carbohydrate-binding (glyco)proteins. The kidney bean lectin phytohaemagglutinin (PHA) of Phaseolus vulgaris (rajma, red kidney bean, also white kidney bean and cannellini) is a tetrameric protein of about 120 kilodaltons with two subunit types, PHA-E (erythroagglutinating) and PHA-L (leucoagglutinating).
Raw red kidney beans contain 20,000 to 70,000 haemagglutinating units (hau) per gram; a properly boiled bean contains 200 to 400 hau. As few as 4 or 5 raw beans can cause illness.
Related lectins: concanavalin A (jack bean), soybean agglutinin, ricin (castor bean; a ribosome-inactivating lectin, not a food lectin but the examiner's favourite comparator).
4.2 Mechanism

Ingested PHA survives gastric acid and proteolysis
        |
        v
Binds oligosaccharide receptors (N-acetylgalactosamine, galactose-rich glycans)
on the brush border of enterocytes
        |
        v
Disrupts microvilli, increases permeability, stimulates hyperplastic crypt
changes, impairs disaccharidase and transporter function
        |
        v
Malabsorption, bacterial overgrowth, fluid secretion, endocytosis of lectin
into the circulation (haemagglutination in vitro)
        |
        v
Nausea, vomiting within 1 to 3 hours, diarrhoea and abdominal pain within hours;
recovery usually in 3 to 4 hours, rarely needs hospitalisation
Chronic feeding of raw beans to animals causes growth depression, loss of nitrogen, pancreatic and intestinal hypertrophy.
4.3 Thermal destruction and the slow-cooker paradox

Lectins are proteins and are denatured by moist heat at 100 degrees Celsius: soak dry beans at least 5 hours, discard the water, then boil vigorously for at least 10 minutes (30 minutes is the conservative recommendation). Pressure cooking is fully effective.

Why slow cooking at sub-boiling temperatures (slow cookers at 70 to 80 degrees Celsius) increases toxicity: partial heating at these temperatures does not unfold PHA but increases its extraction and activity, so the cooked bean can show up to five times the haemagglutinating activity of the raw bean. Dry heat (roasting) and microwave heating of dry beans are also unreliable.
Outbreaks in the United Kingdom were traced to raw or slow-cooked beans in salads and casseroles; canned kidney beans are already retorted and safe.

[HPSC EXAM TRAP] 'Any heating reduces lectin activity' is false. Only temperatures at or above boiling for an adequate time denature PHA; sub-boiling heating increases it. Also, lectin toxicity is a pure protein effect; it is not a cyanide effect and not an allergy.
5. Enzyme Inhibitors: Trypsin and Chymotrypsin Inhibitors
5.1 The two soybean inhibitor families

rows: Single-headed: one site, inhibits trypsin mainly (arginine 63 to isoleucine 64)
Double-headed: one site for trypsin (lysine 16), one for chymotrypsin (leucine 43)
Less stable; destroyed by moist heat
More stable; needs longer heating; survives dry heat
Resistant to gastric acid and pepsin
Share of soy trypsin inhibitor activity

blocks.text: Other legumes (chickpea, pigeon pea, kidney bean, lima bean, groundnut) contain mostly Bowman-Birk type inhibitors; potatoes and cereals contain other serine protease inhibitors.
5.2 Mechanism and pancreatic hypertrophy

Inhibitor forms a tight, slow-dissociating complex with trypsin in the duodenum
        |
        v
Free trypsin falls; protein digestion falls
        |
        v
Loss of trypsin-mediated negative feedback on the intestinal
CCK-releasing peptide (monitor peptide / luminal CCK-releasing factor)
        |
        v
More cholecystokinin (CCK) released from duodenal I cells
        |
        v
Pancreatic acinar cells chronically stimulated: hypersecretion of trypsinogen,
chymotrypsinogen; acinar hypertrophy and hyperplasia (rodents); loss of
sulphur amino acids in secreted enzymes; growth depression
Because pancreatic enzymes are rich in cysteine and methionine, inhibitor-induced hypersecretion drains the limiting sulphur amino acids from a legume diet, aggravating protein deficiency.
Rodents respond with pancreatic hypertrophy; humans and larger animals show hypersecretion but little hypertrophy, so the examiner expects the qualified statement.
5.3 Thermal inactivation dynamics

Inactivation is first order in time and strongly moisture dependent: moist heat at 100 degrees Celsius for 15 to 20 minutes destroys 80 to 90 percent of soybean trypsin inhibitor activity; autoclaving at 120 degrees Celsius for 15 to 30 minutes removes virtually all. Dry roasting at the same temperature is far less effective.
Over-heating causes Maillard loss of lysine, so toasting conditions are optimised to leave a small residual activity (about 10 to 20 percent of raw) while protecting protein quality.

Analytical control: Trypsin Inhibitor Activity assay (benzoyl-DL-arginine-p-nitroanilide substrate), and the indirect urease activity test (change in pH of 0.05 to 0.30 units indicates adequately heated soy meal, because urease and trypsin inhibitor have similar heat sensitivity).
6. Mineral Chelators: Phytic Acid
6.1 The molecule
Phytic acid is myo-inositol 1,2,3,4,5,6-hexakis(dihydrogen phosphate), abbreviated IP6, with six phosphate groups carrying up to 12 negative charges at intestinal pH.

It is the principal phosphorus store of seeds: 1 to 5 percent of cereals, legumes, oilseeds and nuts by dry weight; in wheat and rice it is concentrated in the aleurone layer and bran, in legumes in the cotyledons, and in maize in the germ. Milling of wheat removes much of it; dehulling of legumes removes less.
6.2 Chelation mechanism

Phytate (12 negative charges) + divalent and trivalent cations
(Zn2+, Fe2+ / Fe3+, Ca2+, Mg2+, Cu2+)
        | at the near-neutral pH of the small intestine
        v
Insoluble metal-phytate and protein-metal-phytate ternary complexes
        |
        v
Minerals are not released at the mucosal surface; excreted in faeces
Humans lack sufficient intestinal phytase, so the complexes pass unabsorbed. Zinc is the most affected mineral, iron next, then calcium and magnesium.

Useful predictive ratios: a phytate-to-zinc molar ratio above 15 markedly impairs zinc absorption; a phytate-to-iron molar ratio above 1 impairs non-haem iron absorption; a calcium-times-phytate-to-zinc ratio above 200 is also inhibitory, because calcium potentiates zinc-phytate precipitation.
Phytate also binds proteins (reducing digestibility) and starch, and inhibits alpha-amylase, trypsin and pepsin.
6.3 Degradation by phytase

Phytase (myo-inositol hexakisphosphate phosphohydrolase) sequentially removes phosphate groups to give IP5, IP4, IP3 and ultimately inositol plus inorganic phosphate; only IP6 and IP5 are strongly inhibitory, so even partial dephosphorylation helps.
Plant phytases are 6-phytases (cereals); microbial phytases are mostly 3-phytases (Aspergillus niger). Optimum pH 4.5 to 5.5, optimum temperature 45 to 55 degrees Celsius.

rows: Leaching and activation of endogenous phytase
Strong synthesis and activation of phytase as the seed mobilises phosphorus
Microbial phytase plus acid pH optimum
Phytate is heat-stable; little reduction unless combined with soaking
Physical removal of bran and germ
Large in wheat (80 percent in refined flour)

blocks.text: Enhancers that counter phytate: ascorbic acid, citric acid and meat factors improve iron absorption even in the presence of phytate.
Health note: phytate also has antioxidant and anti-carcinogenic properties in the colon, so a balanced answer mentions that complete elimination is not the goal in a mixed diet.

[HPSC EXAM TRAP] Phytic acid is an antinutrient, not a toxin; the harm is deficiency of zinc, iron and calcium, not direct injury. 'Cooking destroys phytate' is false; 'germination and fermentation reduce phytate' is true.
Part 1B: Other Botanical Toxicants
PART 1B: OTHER BOTANICAL TOXICANTS
1. Solanine and Chaconine: Glycoalkaloids of the Solanaceae
1.1 Chemistry and sources

The two major potato (Solanum tuberosum) glycoalkaloids share the same steroidal aglycone, solanidine (a C27 cholestane-type alkaloid with a nitrogen-containing indolizidine ring). They differ in the trisaccharide at carbon 3:
alpha-Solanine: solatriose (glucose, galactose, rhamnose).
alpha-Chaconine: chacotriose (glucose and two rhamnose units).
alpha-Chaconine is roughly 60 percent of the total and is the more toxic of the two; the pair act synergistically.
Tomato contains alpha-tomatine (aglycone tomatidine), high in green fruit and degraded on ripening; brinjal contains solasonine and solamargine; nightshade berries contain solanine.

Distribution in the potato: concentrated in the peel (30 to 80 percent of the total), in sprouts, eyes and green tissue; a normal tuber contains 20 to 100 mg/kg, a green, sprouted or damaged tuber may exceed 1,000 mg/kg.
Greening is chlorophyll formation under light; the same light also stimulates glycoalkaloid synthesis, so greening is a marker, not the toxin itself.
1.2 Mechanism

Glycoalkaloid
     |
     +--> Inhibits acetylcholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase (reversible)
     |         -> acetylcholine accumulates -> salivation, cramps, bradycardia,
     |            confusion, in severe cases respiratory depression
     |
     +--> Sugar side chain complexes with membrane 3-beta-hydroxysterols
               (cholesterol) -> membrane disruption, leakage
               -> gastrointestinal mucosal damage, haemolysis in vitro
Absorption from the gut is poor, which is why gastrointestinal effects dominate and systemic cholinergic effects appear only at higher doses.
1.3 Clinical pathology

Onset 8 to 12 hours (sometimes 30 minutes to 24 hours): nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, burning throat, headache, fever; severe cases show drowsiness, hallucinations, bradycardia, hypotension, dilated pupils, respiratory failure.
Toxic dose: 2 to 5 mg/kg body weight; potentially lethal at 3 to 6 mg/kg. Classic outbreak: 78 London schoolboys in 1979 from stored potatoes containing about 250 to 300 mg/kg.
1.4 Thermal stability and control

Glycoalkaloids decompose only above 170 degrees Celsius (melting with decomposition near 260 degrees Celsius); boiling, baking and microwaving change them little, since they are not leached in quantity and not destroyed. Deep frying at 170 degrees Celsius or above reduces them partly because of thermal degradation and loss into oil.
Practical control: store tubers in the dark, cool and dry; discard green, sprouted, bitter or damaged tubers; peel thickly (removes 30 to 80 percent); cut out eyes and sprouts.

Safe ceiling: 200 mg total glycoalkaloids per kg fresh weight (20 mg/100 g), the value used by most regulators and plant breeders (new varieties exceeding it are not released); bitterness is detectable at about 140 mg/kg, burning at 200 mg/kg.
[HPSC EXAM TRAP] 'Boiling detoxifies green potatoes' is false. 'Peeling reduces glycoalkaloids' is true. 'The limit is 200 mg/kg for each of solanine and chaconine' is false: 200 mg/kg is the total.
2. Goitrogens and Glucosinolates (Brassica family)
2.1 Chemistry

Glucosinolates are beta-thioglucoside N-hydroxysulphates: a glucose attached through sulphur to a carbon that carries a variable side chain (R) and an N-O-sulphate group. More than 120 occur in the Brassicaceae (Cruciferae): cabbage, cauliflower, mustard, rapeseed, turnip, radish, kale, broccoli.
2.2 Myrosinase hydrolysis

Glucosinolate (in vacuole)  +  myrosinase (thioglucosidase, in separate 'myrosin' cells)
        | tissue disruption by chopping, chewing or insect attack
        v
Glucose + unstable thiohydroximate-O-sulphonate aglycone
        |
        +-- neutral pH -----> isothiocyanate (R-N=C=S)
        +-- acid pH, Fe2+ --> nitrile (R-C=N) and sulphur
        +-- indole or hydroxybenzyl side chain --> thiocyanate ion (SCN-)
        +-- 2-hydroxy side chain (progoitrin) --> isothiocyanate cyclises
                                                  spontaneously to goitrin
                                                  (oxazolidine-2-thione)
Cooking inactivates myrosinase, but intact glucosinolates reaching the colon are hydrolysed by gut bacteria, so cooked cabbage is still mildly goitrogenic.
2.3 Two different antithyroid mechanisms (the examiner's distinction)

rows: Sodium-iodide symporter of the thyroid follicular cell
Competitive inhibition of iodide uptake, which the user's syllabus describes as competitive inhibition of thyroidal iodine uptake
Yes, high iodine intake restores uptake
Blocks organification (iodination of tyrosyl residues of thyroglobulin) and coupling, so thyroxine synthesis falls
No, iodine supplementation does not reverse it (thiourea-like action, similar to propylthiouracil)

blocks.text: Consequences: lowered thyroxine and tri-iodothyronine, raised thyroid stimulating hormone, follicular hyperplasia and goitre. Human goitre from Brassica alone is rare; it becomes significant where iodine intake is marginal (the 'cabbage goitre' of the Himalayan and sub-Himalayan belts, and the cassava-thiocyanate goitre of Central Africa).
Rapeseed meal for animals is limited to about 30 micromoles glucosinolate per gram; low-glucosinolate 'double-zero' canola (low erucic acid, low glucosinolate) was bred for this reason.

Processing: blanching in boiling water leaches soluble glucosinolates (30 to 60 percent into the water) and inactivates myrosinase; fermentation (sauerkraut) hydrolyses them; adequate dietary iodine is the public-health control.
[HPSC EXAM TRAP] Goitrin is formed from progoitrin, not from sinigrin. Sinigrin gives allyl isothiocyanate (the hot taste of mustard). A pair that writes 'sinigrin to goitrin' is false.
3. Oxalates
3.1 Forms and sources

Oxalic acid (ethanedioic acid, HOOC-COOH) occurs as soluble sodium and potassium oxalate in cell sap, and as insoluble calcium oxalate crystals (raphides, needle-shaped bundles; druses; crystal sand).

rows: 500 to 1,300 in stalks; leaves are poisonous
Tea (dry leaf), cocoa, nuts, star fruit

blocks.text: 3.2 Mechanism of harm

Soluble oxalate absorbed (2 to 15 percent of intake)
        |
        v
Binds ionised calcium in blood -> hypocalcaemia (acute, high dose only)
        -> tetany, convulsions, cardiac arrhythmia
        |
        v
Filtered by kidney, precipitates as calcium oxalate monohydrate
(whewellite) in tubules -> acute oxalate nephropathy; chronically,
nucleation of calcium oxalate renal calculi (about 75 percent of all
kidney stones)

Insoluble calcium oxalate (raphides) in colocasia and dieffenbachia
        |
        v
Needles pierce oral mucosa, with proteolytic enzyme co-released
        -> burning, itching, oedema of lips and tongue (acridity), rarely airway oedema

In the gut, dietary oxalate binds calcium and lowers calcium absorption (antinutrient effect); conversely, dietary calcium taken with an oxalate-rich meal binds oxalate in the lumen and reduces oxalate absorption, which is why spinach with paneer or yoghurt is nutritionally rational.
Acute lethal dose of oxalic acid is about 15 to 30 g in adults (not achievable from spinach, but achievable from rhubarb leaves or industrial oxalic acid, the classical 'salt of sorrel' poison).
3.3 Processing

Boiling leaves in a large volume of water and discarding it removes 30 to 90 percent of soluble oxalate (depends on surface area and water volume); steaming removes less; frying removes almost none because there is no aqueous phase.
Cooking colocasia with tamarind, lime or amchur (acid) and with calcium-rich ingredients reduces acridity; adequate boiling softens raphides.
Stone patients are advised to limit high-oxalate foods, drink ample water and not to restrict dietary calcium.

[HPSC EXAM TRAP] Spinach is not a good calcium source despite its high calcium content, because the calcium is largely locked as oxalate. Rhubarb stalks are edible; rhubarb leaves are toxic. 'Frying removes oxalate' is false.
4. Argemone mexicana and Epidemic Dropsy
4.1 The adulterant

Argemone mexicana (prickly poppy, satyanashi, pili kateli, Mexican poppy) grows as a weed in mustard fields. Its seeds resemble black mustard (Brassica nigra) seeds in size and colour and are harvested with the crop or added deliberately because the seed oil is cheap.

Argemone seeds contain 30 to 35 percent of a pale yellow oil rich in the benzophenanthridine (isoquinoline) alkaloids sanguinarine (about 0.3 percent of oil) and its reduced form dihydrosanguinarine (about 1 percent); the seed also contains protopine and berberine. Dihydrosanguinarine is converted to sanguinarine in the body.
Dangerous level: oil containing about 1 percent argemone oil (0.01 percent sanguinarine) causes disease; outbreaks occur with 2 to 10 percent adulteration.
4.2 Mechanism

Sanguinarine (a quaternary benzophenanthridine cation)
        |
        +--> Inhibits Na+/K+-ATPase (ouabain-like) in vascular endothelium
        |       and cardiac muscle -> endothelial swelling, increased capillary
        |       permeability, plasma leakage
        |
        +--> Inhibits pyruvate oxidation and glucose-6-phosphatase, depletes
        |       hepatic glycogen; oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation
        |
        +--> Dilates capillaries and arterioles; pooling of blood
        |
        v
Non-inflammatory, bilateral pitting oedema of the legs, hypoproteinaemia,
high-output cardiac failure, retinal vascular dilatation and haemorrhages,
raised intra-ocular pressure (glaucoma)
4.3 Clinical pathology (epidemic dropsy)
Onset 1 to 3 weeks after eating the adulterated oil; whole households fall ill together, which distinguishes it from cardiac or renal dropsy.
Gastrointestinal prodrome: diarrhoea, vomiting, loss of appetite.
Dropsy: bilateral pitting oedema of the lower limbs that spreads upwards, with erythema, tenderness and a sensation of heat; dilated superficial veins; sarcoid-like skin nodules; hair loss.
Cardiovascular: tachycardia, cardiomegaly, congestive high-output cardiac failure (the main cause of death, mortality 5 percent in outbreaks).
Eyes: glaucoma from raised intra-ocular pressure, retinal haemorrhage and venous dilatation, blurred vision; can cause blindness.
Others: mild anaemia, fever, breathlessness, proteinuria, hepatomegaly.

Major outbreaks: Calcutta 1877 (first description); Delhi 1998 (about 3,000 cases, more than 60 deaths, which triggered the ban on loose sale of edible oil); recurring episodes in Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Gwalior 2000 and 2012.
Treatment is supportive (diuretics, calcium, antioxidants, management of glaucoma); removal of the oil from the diet is curative in survivors.
4.4 Analytical identification

rows: Nitric acid test (Hofmann test, the official qualitative test)
Sanguinarine forms a coloured (red to orange-red) complex with concentrated nitric acid
Shake 5 mL oil with 5 mL concentrated nitric acid in a test tube; a reddish-brown to orange-red colour in the acid layer indicates argemone oil
Shake oil with 10 mL ferric chloride solution, heat in a boiling water bath; precipitate or dark colour indicates argemone
Separation of sanguinarine and dihydrosanguinarine from the oil matrix; the spots fluoresce orange-yellow under ultraviolet light; comparison of Rf with authentic sanguinarine
Extract oil with ethanol, concentrate, spot on Whatman paper, develop, view under ultraviolet
Detects as low as 0.0001 percent (1 ppm)
Thin-layer chromatography and high-performance liquid chromatography
Quantitative estimation of sanguinarine and dihydrosanguinarine
Silica gel plate or reversed-phase column, fluorescence or ultraviolet detection

Argemone seed is black, rough, with a reticulated (net-like) surface, slightly larger than mustard, bitter, and shows a white kernel inside when crushed; mustard seed is smooth with a yellowish kernel

blocks.text: 4.5 Statutory position

Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations, 2011, standard for mustard oil and all edible oils: the test for argemone oil shall be negative; argemone oil is a prohibited adulterant with nil tolerance.

Food Safety and Standards (Prohibition and Restrictions on Sales) Regulations, 2011: prohibition on sale of edible oil adulterated with argemone oil and, since 1998, restriction on sale of loose edible oil (packaged oil must carry the manufacturer's identification).
Under the Act, argemone adulteration that causes injury is treated as unsafe food attracting the severest penalties (Section 59, up to life imprisonment where death results).

[HPSC EXAM TRAP] Epidemic dropsy is not a nutritional oedema (not protein-energy malnutrition) and not a cardiac disease of the individual; it is a poisoning that affects a whole family. The screening test is nitric acid (0.25 percent); the confirmatory and most sensitive test is paper chromatography (0.0001 percent). A pair reversing these sensitivities is false.
Part 2: Marine & Animal Biotoxins
PART 2: MARINE AND ANIMAL BIOTOXINS
First-principles orientation

Most marine biotoxins are made not by the animal eaten but by microscopic planktonic algae (dinoflagellates and diatoms) or by bacteria. Filter-feeding bivalves (mussels, clams, oysters, scallops) concentrate the algae; reef fish concentrate algal toxins through the food chain; pufferfish concentrate bacterial toxin. Nearly all of these toxins are small, water-soluble or lipid-soluble molecules that are heat-stable, tasteless and odourless, so cooking is useless and the only control is monitoring of harvesting waters and the product. The majority act on ion channels or signalling enzymes of nerve and muscle, which is why the clinical pictures are neurological.
Shared background: the voltage-gated sodium channel
Nerve conduction and muscle contraction depend on the rapid opening of voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav). Toxins bind at numbered receptor sites:
Site 1 (outer pore mouth): saxitoxin and tetrodotoxin plug the pore and block sodium entry; the nerve cannot fire; result is flaccid paralysis.

Site 5 (transmembrane segments): brevetoxins and ciguatoxins bind, shift activation to more negative potentials and prevent inactivation; the channel opens persistently; result is repetitive firing, paraesthesiae and the temperature-reversal sensation.
1. Shellfish Poisoning Syndromes
1.1 Paralytic Shellfish Poisoning (PSP)

rows: Saxitoxin (STX) and more than 50 analogues (gonyautoxins, neosaxitoxin, decarbamoyl and sulphocarbamoyl derivatives); saxitoxin is a tricyclic tetrahydropurine with two guanidinium groups, water-soluble, heat-stable, acid-stable, destroyed by alkali
Marine dinoflagellates Alexandrium (catenella, tamarense, minutum; formerly Gonyaulax), Gymnodinium catenatum, Pyrodinium bahamense; also freshwater cyanobacteria (Anabaena, Aphanizomenon)
Mussels, clams, oysters, scallops, cockles; also crabs, lobsters, gastropods that feed on contaminated bivalves

Reversible, high-affinity block of site 1 of the voltage-gated sodium channel of nerve and skeletal muscle; conduction fails; neuromuscular transmission and respiratory muscle contraction stop; cardiac muscle is relatively spared
One of the most potent known non-protein toxins: lethal oral dose about 1 to 4 mg (about 10 to 20 micrograms per kg); 5 to 30 micrograms per kg causes symptoms

Onset 5 to 30 minutes, up to 2 hours: tingling and numbness of lips, tongue and face spreading to limbs; floating sensation, headache, dizziness, incoordination, dysarthria; in severe cases muscle weakness progressing to respiratory paralysis within 2 to 12 hours; consciousness preserved; mortality 1 to 15 percent, mainly within 12 hours if ventilation is not provided; survivors recover fully
No antidote; mechanical ventilation, gastric lavage, activated charcoal, supportive care
80 micrograms STX equivalents per 100 g shellfish meat (0.8 mg/kg), the Codex and worldwide standard

Mouse bioassay (AOAC official method; 1 mouse unit = dose killing a 20 g mouse in 15 minutes), replaced progressively by high-performance liquid chromatography with pre- or post-column oxidation and fluorescence detection (Lawrence method), liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, receptor-binding assay

blocks.text: 1.2 Diarrhetic Shellfish Poisoning (DSP)

rows: Okadaic acid (OA) and dinophysistoxins (DTX-1, DTX-2, DTX-3), lipophilic polyether fatty acids; heat-stable; often co-occur with pectenotoxins and yessotoxins
Dinoflagellates Dinophysis (acuta, fortii, acuminata) and benthic Prorocentrum lima
Mussels, scallops, clams; toxin concentrates in the hepatopancreas (digestive gland)

Potent, specific inhibition of the serine/threonine protein phosphatases PP2A (most strongly) and PP1; proteins that control cytoskeleton, ion transport and secretion remain hyperphosphorylated; in enterocytes this causes loss of tight-junction integrity, increased paracellular permeability and secretion of fluid and electrolytes; okadaic acid is also a tumour promoter (phosphatase inhibition activates proliferation pathways)

Onset 30 minutes to a few hours (usually within 12 hours): profuse diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, chills; self-limiting within 3 days; no fatalities recorded; chronic exposure suspected to promote gastrointestinal tumours
European Union: 160 micrograms okadaic acid equivalents per kg whole flesh; Codex: 0.16 mg/kg
Mouse bioassay (historical), protein phosphatase inhibition assay, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (reference method)

blocks.text: 1.3 Neurotoxic Shellfish Poisoning (NSP)

rows: Brevetoxins (PbTx-1 to PbTx-10), lipid-soluble cyclic polyether ladder molecules; heat-stable
Dinoflagellate Karenia brevis (formerly Gymnodinium breve, Ptychodiscus brevis), the Florida and Gulf of Mexico 'red tide' organism; also New Zealand
Oysters, clams, mussels; unusual feature: aerosolised toxin in sea spray during blooms causes respiratory irritation on beaches; also massive fish and manatee kills

Binds site 5 of the voltage-gated sodium channel; opens the channel at resting potential and blocks inactivation; persistent sodium influx, membrane depolarisation and repetitive firing; release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction

Onset 30 minutes to 3 hours: paraesthesiae of mouth and limbs, temperature reversal sensation (shared with ciguatera), gastrointestinal upset, ataxia, dizziness, bradycardia or tachycardia, dilated pupils; no deaths recorded; recovery within days; inhalation causes cough, bronchoconstriction, conjunctival irritation
20 mouse units per 100 g (about 0.8 mg PbTx-2 equivalents per kg) in the United States
Mouse bioassay, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, receptor-binding assay, liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry

blocks.text: 1.4 Amnesic Shellfish Poisoning (ASP)

rows: Domoic acid, a water-soluble tricarboxylic amino acid of the kainoid class (structural analogue of glutamate and kainic acid); heat-stable
Diatoms, not dinoflagellates: Pseudo-nitzschia (multiseries, australis, pungens); also the red alga Chondria armata (from which it was first isolated as an anthelmintic in Japan)
Mussels, razor clams, scallops, crabs; also anchovies and sardines, through which sea lions and sea birds are poisoned

Potent agonist at ionotropic glutamate receptors, particularly kainate and AMPA receptors; sustained excitation, calcium overload and excitotoxic neuronal death, concentrated in the hippocampus (CA1 and CA3 regions) and amygdala, the brain regions responsible for forming new memories; the blood-brain barrier is crossed poorly, so the very young and the elderly with leakier barriers are most affected

Onset 15 minutes to 38 hours: vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal cramps; then headache, confusion, disorientation, seizures, coma; survivors show permanent anterograde amnesia (loss of short-term memory), peripheral neuropathy and seizures; first recognised in the Prince Edward Island (Canada) outbreak of 1987 from blue mussels: 107 cases, 3 deaths, 12 with lasting memory loss
20 mg domoic acid per kg (20 micrograms per gram) of shellfish meat, Codex and worldwide

High-performance liquid chromatography with ultraviolet detection at 242 nm (the AOAC reference method), liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay; the mouse bioassay is insensitive

blocks.text: [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Three traps in one table: (1) ASP is from a diatom, the other three are from dinoflagellates; (2) saxitoxin blocks the sodium channel, brevetoxin opens it; (3) okadaic acid does not act on an ion channel at all, it inhibits protein phosphatases. A fourth: PSP and ASP limits are both expressed per mass but in different units, 80 micrograms per 100 g versus 20 mg per kg.
2. Finfish Toxins
2.1 Ciguatera Fish Poisoning (CFP)

rows: Ciguatoxins (CTX; Pacific P-CTX-1 is the most potent, Caribbean C-CTX-1), lipid-soluble cyclic polyether ladders; maitotoxin (MTX), the largest and most potent non-protein toxin known, water-soluble; also scaritoxin and gambierol
Benthic dinoflagellate Gambierdiscus toxicus and related species living as epiphytes on dead coral and macroalgae in tropical reefs between 35 degrees north and 35 degrees south latitude

Gambierdiscus produces gambiertoxins; herbivorous reef fish (surgeonfish, parrotfish) graze the algae; carnivorous reef fish eat the herbivores; toxins are oxidised in the fish liver into more potent ciguatoxins and biomagnified; the largest, oldest predators are most toxic: barracuda, grouper, red snapper, amberjack, moray eel, Spanish mackerel, coral trout; viscera (liver, roe) carry most toxin

Ciguatoxin binds site 5 of the voltage-gated sodium channel (same site as brevetoxin but with higher affinity), causing persistent activation at resting potential, spontaneous and repetitive action potentials in sensory nerves and swelling of nodes of Ranvier; maitotoxin activates non-selective cation channels and calcium entry, causing calcium-dependent cell damage

Onset 1 to 24 hours (usually 2 to 6 hours). Gastrointestinal phase: vomiting, diarrhoea, cramps. Neurological phase: circumoral and extremity paraesthesiae, pruritus, myalgia, arthralgia, and the pathognomonic temperature reversal dysaesthesia or cold allodynia (cold objects feel hot or burning and hot feels cold, because persistently activated cold-sensitive fibres misfire); metallic taste, dental pain, blurred vision. Cardiovascular: bradycardia, hypotension. Symptoms persist for weeks to months and may be reactivated by alcohol, nuts or fish; mortality below 0.5 percent; ciguatera is the commonest non-bacterial fish-borne illness worldwide (10,000 to 50,000 cases per year)

Toxins are heat-stable, freeze-stable, tasteless and not removed by drying, salting or smoking; no visual or sensory test; avoid large predatory reef fish and their viscera; mouse bioassay, receptor-binding assay, cytotoxicity assay and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry; United States guidance level 0.01 micrograms P-CTX-1 equivalents per kg fish; intravenous mannitol has been used empirically for neurological symptoms

blocks.text: 2.2 Scombroid (Histamine) Poisoning

rows: Dark-fleshed, fast-swimming fish with high free histidine in muscle: family Scombridae (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack, seer fish) and non-scombroid species such as sardine, anchovy, mahi-mahi (dolphin fish), bluefish, herring, marlin

Free L-histidine is decarboxylated to histamine by bacterial histidine decarboxylase (a pyridoxal-phosphate dependent enzyme); the bacteria are normal gut and gill flora, mainly Gram-negative enteric organisms: Morganella morganii (the strongest producer), Klebsiella pneumoniae, Hafnia alvei, Enterobacter aerogenes, Proteus, Raoultella; also Photobacterium at low temperature; fastest at 20 to 30 degrees Celsius; production is negligible below 4 degrees Celsius but, once formed, histamine and the enzyme persist

Histamine acts directly on H1 and H2 receptors of blood vessels, bronchi, gut and skin, reproducing the picture of an immunoglobulin E mediated allergic reaction without any antibody; it occurs in people with no fish allergy, affects several people eating the same fish, and responds to antihistamines; co-amines in spoiled fish (cadaverine, putrescine) inhibit intestinal diamine oxidase and potentiate histamine; this is why gut-wall inactivation fails and why patients on isoniazid or monoamine oxidase inhibitors are more sensitive

Onset 10 minutes to 2 hours: flushing of face and neck, urticaria, pruritus, headache, palpitations, burning or peppery taste, oral tingling, nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, hypotension, bronchospasm; resolves within 12 to 24 hours; rarely fatal; treated with antihistamines (H1 and H2 blockers)

Histamine is heat-stable: cooking, canning, smoking, freezing and retorting do not destroy it; canned tuna is a classic vehicle; sensory spoilage signs may be absent, so the fish can taste normal (sometimes peppery or honeycombed flesh)

Codex Standard for fish and fishery products: no sample above 100 mg/kg histamine as a hygiene indicator; 200 mg/kg as the decomposition limit; European Union: two-class sampling plan with 100 mg/kg (m) and 200 mg/kg (M) in fresh fish, 200 and 400 mg/kg in enzyme-ripened products; United States Food and Drug Administration action level 50 mg/kg (because this level indicates that parts of the lot may exceed 500 mg/kg); FSSAI standard for fish and fishery products specifies a histamine ceiling of 200 mg/kg for histamine-prone species (confirm against the current gazette)

AOAC fluorometric method (histamine condensed with o-phthaldialdehyde), enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay rapid kits, high-performance liquid chromatography; prevention by rapid chilling below 4 degrees Celsius within hours of catch (time-temperature control, the critical control point in the HACCP plan for tuna)

blocks.text: 2.3 Tetrodotoxin (TTX)

rows: Pufferfish (fugu) of the family Tetraodontidae (Takifugu, Fugu, Lagocephalus), porcupine fish (Diodontidae), ocean sunfish, blue-ringed octopus, certain newts (Taricha), toads (Atelopus), xanthid crabs, horseshoe crab eggs, some gastropods

Produced by symbiotic and gut bacteria (Vibrio alginolyticus, Vibrio fischeri, Pseudomonas, Shewanella, Alteromonas, Bacillus) and accumulated through the food chain; cultured pufferfish fed a toxin-free diet are non-toxic, which proves the exogenous origin; the fish is resistant because its own sodium channels carry a mutation (aromatic residue substitution in domain I) that prevents toxin binding
Highest in ovary and liver, then intestine, skin; muscle of most species is nearly toxin-free, which is the basis of licensed fugu preparation in Japan
Aminoperhydroquinazoline with a guanidinium group and a hemilactal; heat-stable, water-soluble, stable to cooking but destroyed by strong alkali

Binds site 1 of the voltage-gated sodium channel from the outside and plugs the pore (the guanidinium group mimics the hydrated sodium ion); pharmacologically identical to saxitoxin; blocks conduction in sensory and motor nerves and skeletal muscle; does not cross the blood-brain barrier well, so consciousness is retained

Onset 10 to 45 minutes (up to 3 hours): perioral numbness and tingling; salivation, nausea; then ascending flaccid paralysis: limbs, trunk, respiratory muscles; aphonia, dysphagia, fixed dilated pupils, hypotension, bradycardia; death by respiratory failure within 4 to 6 hours in 50 to 60 percent of untreated severe cases; patients may appear dead while fully conscious ('zombie' phenomenon); lethal dose about 1 to 2 mg, about 10 times more toxic than cyanide by weight; four grades of severity are used clinically
No antidote; early gastric lavage, activated charcoal, mechanical ventilation; if ventilated through the first 24 hours, recovery is complete

In India, sale of pufferfish for food is not standardised and is effectively prohibited; Japan licenses fugu chefs who remove ovary, liver and skin; mouse bioassay (Japanese official method; limit 10 mouse units per gram, about 2 mg/kg), high-performance liquid chromatography with post-column fluorescence, liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry

blocks.text: [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Tetrodotoxin and saxitoxin have the same mechanism (site 1 block) but different origins: tetrodotoxin is bacterial via the pufferfish, saxitoxin is dinoflagellate via shellfish. 'Tetrodotoxin is produced by the pufferfish itself' is false. 'Scombroid poisoning can be prevented by cooking' is false; it is prevented by chilling the fish quickly after catch. 'Ciguatera fish look or taste abnormal' is false.
Part 3A: Heavy Metals
PART 3A: HEAVY METALS AND TOXIC TRACE ELEMENTS
First-principles orientation

Heavy metals are not metabolised and not destroyed by cooking; the body can only excrete them slowly. Harm therefore depends on cumulative body burden, on the chemical species (ionic, organic, valence) that determines absorption and target organ, and on the age of the consumer (children absorb more lead, foetuses are more sensitive to methylmercury). Three mechanisms recur: (1) binding to sulphydryl groups of enzymes, (2) displacement of essential metals (lead for calcium and zinc, cadmium for zinc and calcium, arsenate for phosphate), and (3) oxidative stress. The analytical backbone is the same for all: acid digestion (microwave) followed by atomic absorption spectrometry (flame, graphite furnace, hydride generation for arsenic, cold vapour for mercury) or inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry.
Statutory framework

Food Safety and Standards (Contaminants, Toxins and Residues) Regulations, 2011, Regulation 2.1 (Metal Contaminants), as harmonised with Codex by the 2018 to 2020 amendments: commodity-specific maximum limits in mg/kg (parts per million) for lead, cadmium, mercury, methylmercury, arsenic, tin, copper, zinc, nickel and chromium.
Section 3(1)(zz) of the Act: food is unsafe if it contains contaminants beyond specified limits.

Codex General Standard for Contaminants and Toxins in Food and Feed (CXS 193-1995) is the international reference; JECFA sets Provisional Tolerable Weekly Intakes (PTWI) or Provisional Tolerable Monthly Intakes (PTMI).
1. Lead (Pb)
1.1 Sources in food

Leaded petrol (historical), lead-based paints, lead-soldered cans, lead-glazed ceramics (acidic foods such as pickles, fruit juices and curd leach lead), brass and bronze utensils, lead water pipes, contaminated soil and irrigation water near smelters and battery recycling, lead chromate adulteration of turmeric and spices, calcium supplements from bone meal, and dust deposition on leafy vegetables grown by roadsides.
Children absorb 40 to 50 percent of ingested lead; adults 10 to 15 percent; absorption rises with iron, calcium and zinc deficiency and with fasting.
1.2 Mechanism: the haem synthesis block

Succinyl-CoA + glycine
        | delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase (mitochondria)
        v
Delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA)  <-- accumulates and spills into urine (neurotoxic itself)
        | delta-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase (ALAD), a zinc enzyme
        | *** INHIBITED BY LEAD (lead displaces zinc from the active-site cysteines) ***
        v
Porphobilinogen -> ... -> coproporphyrinogen III (coproporphyrin rises in urine)
        |
        v
Protoporphyrin IX
        | ferrochelatase (mitochondrial, inserts Fe2+)
        | *** INHIBITED BY LEAD ***
        v
Haem   <-- falls; zinc protoporphyrin (ZPP) and free erythrocyte protoporphyrin rise

Result: microcytic hypochromic anaemia (haem synthesis fails despite adequate iron), shortened red cell survival, and basophilic stippling of red cells (lead inhibits pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase, so ribosomal RNA fragments persist).
ALAD inhibition is the most sensitive biochemical marker; zinc protoporphyrin is the screening marker; blood lead is the definitive measure.
1.3 Neurological and other toxicity
Lead mimics calcium: it enters neurons through calcium channels, interferes with neurotransmitter release, activates protein kinase C, and disrupts the blood-brain barrier.

Children: irreversible loss of intelligence quotient (about 1 to 3 points per 10 micrograms per decilitre at low levels), behavioural problems, hearing loss, growth retardation; acute encephalopathy with cerebral oedema and convulsions above about 70 micrograms per decilitre. No threshold is considered safe; the United States reference value for action is 3.5 micrograms per decilitre.

Adults: peripheral motor neuropathy (wrist drop, foot drop), lead colic (abdominal pain, constipation), Burton's blue line on the gums, nephropathy (proximal tubular damage, gout, chronic kidney disease), hypertension, reduced fertility, and in pregnancy, miscarriage and low birth weight; lead stored in bone is mobilised during pregnancy and lactation.
JECFA withdrew the PTWI of 25 micrograms per kg body weight in 2010 because no safe level could be identified.
Treatment: remove the source; chelation with calcium disodium edetate, dimercaprol or succimer (dimercaptosuccinic acid) in symptomatic or high-level cases.
1.4 Representative FSSAI limits for lead (mg/kg)

rows: Milk; infant formula and infant foods
Packaged drinking water and natural mineral water

blocks.text: 2. Cadmium (Cd)
2.1 Sources

Phosphate fertilisers (cadmium is a natural contaminant of rock phosphate), sewage sludge, zinc and lead smelting and mining effluent, electroplating, nickel-cadmium batteries, cigarette smoke (1 to 2 micrograms per cigarette; smokers have double the body burden).

Plants take up cadmium readily: rice (especially in flooded paddies irrigated with contaminated water), wheat, leafy vegetables, potatoes; the richest animal sources are kidney and liver, and the hepatopancreas of crustaceans and cephalopods (crab brown meat, squid), and oysters and mussels. Cocoa and chocolate are also notable.
2.2 Mechanism

Ingested Cd2+ (absorption 3 to 5 percent, higher with iron deficiency, as cadmium
uses the divalent metal transporter DMT1)
        |
        v
Liver synthesises metallothionein (cysteine-rich, binds Cd as Cd-MT)
        |
        v
Cd-MT released into blood, freely filtered by the glomerulus, reabsorbed by
proximal tubular cells, degraded in lysosomes, releasing free Cd2+
        |
        v
When tubular metallothionein capacity is exceeded (renal cortex above about
200 micrograms per gram), free Cd2+ binds sulphydryl enzymes, generates oxidative
stress and triggers apoptosis of proximal tubular cells
        |
        v
Irreversible proximal tubular dysfunction: low-molecular-weight proteinuria
(beta-2-microglobulin, retinol-binding protein), glucosuria, aminoaciduria,
phosphaturia, calciuria (a Fanconi-like syndrome)
        |
        v
Loss of phosphate and calcium, reduced renal activation of vitamin D
(1-alpha-hydroxylase), plus direct cadmium inhibition of osteoblasts and
substitution for calcium in bone mineral
        |
        v
Osteomalacia and osteoporosis, bone demineralisation, multiple pseudofractures
Biological half-life is 10 to 30 years; the kidney and liver hold about half the body burden; the critical organ is the renal cortex.
Cadmium is classified as a Group 1 human carcinogen (lung, prostate, kidney) by the International Agency for Research on Cancer.
JECFA PTMI: 25 micrograms per kg body weight per month (set in 2010, replacing the PTWI of 7 micrograms per kg per week).
2.3 Itai-Itai disease

'Itai-itai' means 'ouch-ouch', from the cries of pain of patients. Occurred in the Jinzu River basin, Toyama Prefecture, Japan, from the 1910s and recognised in 1955 to 1968; caused by cadmium discharged from the Mitsui Mining and Smelting zinc mine at Kamioka into irrigation water, concentrated in rice.

Victims were mainly post-menopausal multiparous women with low calcium and vitamin D status: severe bone pain, waddling gait, spontaneous fractures of ribs and pelvis, skeletal deformity, height loss, renal tubular dysfunction, anaemia; many were bedridden.
It was the first case of pollution-related disease legally recognised in Japan (1968), the lesson being that environmental cadmium reaches humans through the staple crop.
2.4 Representative FSSAI limits for cadmium (mg/kg)

rows: 0.1 (Indian value; Codex allows 0.4; verify current notification)
Wheat; cereal grains other than rice and wheat

blocks.text: 3. Mercury (Hg)
3.1 Three chemical forms, three toxicities

rows: Vapour inhaled, 80 percent absorbed by lung; almost nil absorbed from the gut if swallowed (less than 0.01 percent), so a swallowed thermometer bulb is harmless
Brain (crosses blood-brain barrier as vapour, oxidised to Hg2+ by catalase and trapped), kidney
Dental amalgam, thermometers, chlor-alkali plants, gold panning
7 to 15 percent absorbed from gut; corrosive
Skin-lightening creams, disinfectants, 'calomel' teething powders (historical pink disease, acrodynia)
95 percent absorbed from gut; lipophilic; bound to cysteine it mimics methionine and crosses the blood-brain barrier and the placenta by the large neutral amino acid transporter
Central nervous system, especially cerebellum, visual cortex, developing foetal brain
Fish and shellfish, fungicide-treated seed grain (Iraq 1971 to 1972, 6,500 cases)

blocks.text: 3.2 How fish become the source: biomethylation and biomagnification

Inorganic mercury from industrial effluent, coal combustion, gold mining,
volcanoes deposited in water and sediment
        | sulphate-reducing and iron-reducing bacteria in anoxic sediment
        v
Methylmercury (CH3Hg+), lipophilic, binds tightly to cysteine in fish muscle protein
        |
        v
Plankton -> small fish -> larger fish -> top predators
(biomagnification by a factor of 10 to 100,000; mercury in fish is 90 to 100 percent
methylmercury and cannot be removed by cooking, trimming or washing)
        |
        v
Highest in large, long-lived, predatory, pelagic fish: shark, swordfish, king
mackerel, tilefish, bigeye tuna, marlin; lowest in sardine, anchovy, pomfret,
small mackerel, shrimp, salmon, tilapia
3.3 Mechanism

Methylmercury has extreme affinity for sulphydryl groups; it binds tubulin and disrupts microtubules (so neuronal migration in the foetal brain fails), inhibits protein synthesis, depletes glutathione, causes oxidative damage and disturbs calcium homeostasis and neurotransmitter release.
The adult brain lesion is focal (cerebellar granule cells, calcarine visual cortex, dorsal root ganglia); the foetal lesion is diffuse because migration is disrupted everywhere.
3.4 Clinical pathology and Minamata disease

Adult methylmercury poisoning (Hunter-Russell syndrome, 1940): paraesthesiae of lips and fingers, constriction of visual fields (tunnel vision), cerebellar ataxia, dysarthria, deafness, tremor, cognitive decline; latency weeks to months, dose-dependent.

Minamata disease: Minamata Bay, Kumamoto, Japan; the Chisso Corporation's acetaldehyde plant used mercuric sulphate as catalyst and discharged methylmercury in effluent from 1932 to 1968; fish and shellfish in the bay accumulated it; the disease was recognised in 1956 (cats 'dancing' and dying first); more than 2,200 officially certified patients, more than 1,700 deaths, and thousands more affected; a second outbreak at Niigata (Agano River, Showa Denko) in 1965.

Congenital (foetal) Minamata disease: mothers with little or no symptoms gave birth to children with cerebral palsy-like syndromes, microcephaly, mental retardation, seizures, blindness and deafness, proving that the foetus is far more sensitive than the mother; this is the basis of fish-consumption advisories for pregnant women.
JECFA PTWI for methylmercury: 1.6 micrograms per kg body weight per week (foetal protection); for total mercury 4 micrograms per kg per week.
Minamata Convention on Mercury (2013, in force 2017; India ratified in 2018) phases out mercury products and controls emissions.
3.5 Representative FSSAI limits for mercury (mg/kg)

rows: Large predatory fish (shark, swordfish, tuna, marlin, pike)

blocks.text: 4. Arsenic (As)
4.1 Species and sources

rows: Most toxic (about 60 times more than As(V)); binds vicinal dithiols
Groundwater, soil, pesticide-treated land (lead arsenate, historical)
Intermediate; trivalent methylated forms are highly toxic
Formed in liver; also in rice
Fish and shellfish (this is why total arsenic in fish is high but harmless, and why limits for seafood refer to inorganic arsenic or are set higher)

blocks.text: Groundwater: the Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna delta is the world's largest arsenic calamity: West Bengal (Murshidabad, Nadia, North and South 24 Parganas), Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Assam, Jharkhand and Bangladesh, where shallow tube wells tap arsenic-rich alluvial aquifers (geogenic release from iron oxyhydroxides under reducing conditions).

Rice: grown in flooded (anaerobic) paddies, which keep arsenic in the mobile As(III) form; rice roots take up arsenite through the silicon transporters Lsi1 and Lsi2, so rice accumulates ten times more arsenic than other cereals; bran and husk contain the most, so brown rice has more than polished rice; cooking in excess arsenic-free water and discarding it removes 30 to 60 percent, but cooking in arsenic-contaminated water adds arsenic.
4.2 Mechanism

Arsenite, As(III)
        | binds vicinal (paired) sulphydryl groups of dihydrolipoamide in the
        | pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complexes
        v
Blocks entry of pyruvate into the citric acid cycle; ATP production falls;
also binds keratin (hair, nails, skin), inhibits glutathione reductase and
thioredoxin reductase, generates reactive oxygen species, inhibits DNA repair

Arsenate, As(V)
        | chemically mimics phosphate (PO4 3-)
        v
Substitutes for phosphate in glycolysis (1-arseno-3-phosphoglycerate forms
instead of 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate and hydrolyses spontaneously: 'arsenolysis'),
uncoupling ATP synthesis; is reduced in vivo to arsenite

Hepatic methylation (arsenic methyltransferase, using S-adenosylmethionine) was once considered detoxification; trivalent methylated intermediates are now known to be genotoxic and to inhibit enzymes more strongly than arsenite.
4.3 Clinical pathology

Acute poisoning (rare from food): garlic odour, severe cholera-like watery diarrhoea (rice-water stools), vomiting, hypotension, cardiac arrhythmia (QT prolongation), haemolysis, delirium, death; lethal dose of arsenic trioxide about 100 to 300 mg; delayed peripheral neuropathy in survivors; Mees' lines (transverse white bands) on nails 4 to 6 weeks later.

Chronic arsenicosis (the public health problem): raindrop pigmentation (hyper- and hypopigmented spots on trunk), palmoplantar hyperkeratosis, Bowen's disease, skin cancer (squamous and basal cell), lung and bladder cancer (Group 1 carcinogen), peripheral neuropathy, blackfoot disease (gangrene of toes from peripheral vascular disease, Taiwan), hepatomegaly and portal fibrosis, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, reduced intelligence in children.

JECFA withdrew the PTWI of 15 micrograms per kg in 2010; the benchmark dose lower limit for 0.5 percent increased lung cancer is 3 micrograms per kg per day, within the range of dietary exposures in affected regions.

Treatment: dimercaprol or succimer for acute poisoning; for chronic exposure, provision of arsenic-free water (deep aquifers, surface water, arsenic removal plants using iron co-precipitation and adsorption) is the only effective measure.
4.4 Statutory limits for arsenic (mg/kg)

rows: Packaged drinking water and natural mineral water
0.01 mg/L; Bureau of Indian Standards drinking water acceptable limit 0.01 mg/L (permissible in absence of alternative source 0.05 mg/L)
0.1 (older general ceiling; harmonised values lower, verify)
1.0 (older total arsenic value, reflecting non-toxic arsenobetaine)

blocks.text: 5. Tin (Sn)
5.1 Why tin appears in food

Tinplate is steel coated with a thin layer of tin, used for cans because tin is corrosion-resistant and non-toxic at low levels. Inorganic tin is poorly absorbed (less than 5 percent) and has low systemic toxicity, but high concentrations irritate the gut.

Detinning (dissolution of tin into the food) is accelerated by: acidic foods (fruit juices, tomato products, pineapple, rhubarb, pickles; pH below 4), nitrate in the food (from fertilised vegetables and water; nitrate acts as a cathodic depolariser and is the single most important accelerator), oxidising agents, residual oxygen in the headspace, sulphur-containing foods, long storage at high temperature, and opened cans left in the refrigerator (air enters and corrosion accelerates sharply).

Acid + nitrate + dissolved oxygen in canned food
        |
        v
Anodic dissolution of the tin coating: Sn -> Sn2+ + 2 electrons
(tin sacrificially protects the underlying steel, which is cathodic)
        |
        v
Stannous ions in the food, rising with storage time and temperature;
hydrogen gas from steel exposure can swell the can ('hydrogen swell',
a non-microbial swell to be distinguished from microbial spoilage)

Control: internal lacquering (epoxy-phenolic, vinyl, polyester enamel) of cans for acidic and nitrate-rich foods, low-nitrate raw materials, exclusion of oxygen (hot filling, vacuum closing), cool storage, and transfer of opened can contents to glass or plastic.
5.2 Toxicity

Acute gastrointestinal irritation (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, headache) within 30 minutes to 2 hours when food contains more than about 200 mg/kg tin; recovery is rapid; no chronic effect from inorganic tin at dietary levels; organotins (tributyltin, used as antifouling paint) are far more toxic and are a separate environmental issue.
JECFA PTWI for inorganic tin: 14 mg per kg body weight per week.
5.3 Statutory ceilings

rows: Canned foods (processed and canned products, general)
Canned beverages, including canned fruit juices and nectars
150 mg/kg (Codex, adopted by FSSAI in the harmonised amendment)
Infant foods (Codex guidance for canned baby foods)

blocks.text: [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Tin's statutory ceiling (250 mg/kg) is enormous compared with lead (0.02 to 0.3 mg/kg) because inorganic tin is poorly absorbed and only locally irritant; a pair asserting that tin is 'as toxic as lead' is false. The accelerator to remember for detinning is nitrate, not sugar. A 'hydrogen swell' is chemical, not microbial.

Bone marrow (haem), brain, kidney, peripheral nerve

PART 3B: AGROCHEMICAL RESIDUES, VETERINARY DRUGS AND PROCESS-INDUCED CONTAMINANTS
1. Pesticide Classes
1.1 Organochlorines

rows: Banned for agriculture since 1989; permitted only for public health vector control (malaria, kala-azar)
Metabolites DDE and DDD; half-life in soil 2 to 15 years; eggshell thinning in raptors; Stockholm Convention persistent organic pollutant
BHC or HCH (hexachlorocyclohexane; the gamma isomer is lindane)
Classic contaminant of milk, butter and ghee in Indian surveys
Banned by Supreme Court order 2011, phased out
Aldrin, dieldrin, chlordane, heptachlor, endrin, toxaphene
All Stockholm Convention persistent organic pollutants

blocks.text: Properties: highly lipophilic, chemically stable, resistant to biodegradation, hence persistent in soil and water, bioaccumulate in adipose tissue and biomagnify through the food chain; excreted in milk, so they contaminate dairy fat and breast milk.

Mechanism: DDT holds the voltage-gated sodium channel open (repetitive firing, tremor, convulsions); cyclodienes (aldrin, dieldrin, endosulfan) and lindane antagonise the GABA-A chloride channel (loss of inhibition, seizures). Chronic effects: endocrine disruption (DDE is anti-androgenic), liver enzyme induction, suspected carcinogenicity (DDT Group 2A, lindane Group 1).
Analysis: fat extraction, clean-up by gel permeation or florisil, gas chromatography with electron capture detector.
1.2 Organophosphates

rows: Low mammalian toxicity because mammalian carboxylesterases hydrolyse it; used for grain storage and public health
Widely used; neurodevelopmental concerns; European Union withdrew approval 2020; MRLs reduced
Highly toxic (Class I); monocrotophos caused the Bihar mid-day meal deaths of 2013 (23 children)
Common on vegetables and fruits in Indian monitoring

blocks.text: Mechanism of acetylcholinesterase inhibition:

Organophosphate (phosphorothioate, P=S) 
        | hepatic cytochrome P450 oxidative desulphuration (bioactivation)
        v
Oxon (P=O), the active inhibitor
        |
        v
Phosphorylates the serine hydroxyl of the esteratic site of acetylcholinesterase
(covalent, initially reversible by oximes)
        |
        v
'Ageing': loss of an alkyl group from the phosphorylated enzyme within hours to days
(minutes for soman, 24 to 48 hours for most insecticides); the bond becomes
irreversible; recovery needs new enzyme synthesis (weeks)
        |
        v
Acetylcholine accumulates at muscarinic, nicotinic and central synapses

Clinical picture: muscarinic (DUMBELS: diarrhoea, urination, miosis, bronchorrhoea and bronchospasm, emesis, lacrimation, salivation; bradycardia), nicotinic (fasciculations, weakness, respiratory muscle paralysis, tachycardia), central (anxiety, confusion, seizures, coma). Death from respiratory failure. Intermediate syndrome (proximal weakness 1 to 4 days later) and organophosphate-induced delayed polyneuropathy (2 to 3 weeks later, from inhibition of neuropathy target esterase).
Treatment: decontamination, atropine (muscarinic antagonist, titrated to drying of secretions), pralidoxime (2-PAM; reactivates the enzyme if given before ageing), diazepam for seizures.
Biomarker: red cell cholinesterase (true acetylcholinesterase) and plasma pseudocholinesterase depression.
Analysis: QuEChERS extraction (quick, easy, cheap, effective, rugged, safe), gas chromatography with flame photometric or nitrogen-phosphorus detector, liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry.
1.3 Carbamates
Examples: carbofuran, carbaryl, aldicarb (the most toxic; the 'Temik' poisoning of watermelons, California 1985), methomyl, propoxur, thiodicarb, carbosulfan.

Mechanism: carbamylate the same serine of acetylcholinesterase, but the carbamyl-enzyme bond hydrolyses spontaneously within minutes to hours; no ageing; so inhibition is reversible and short-lived, symptoms are similar but briefer, central effects are less (poor blood-brain barrier penetration).
Treatment: atropine; pralidoxime is not generally recommended (and was historically thought to worsen carbaryl toxicity) because the enzyme recovers on its own.
Environmental fate: not persistent, water-soluble, do not bioaccumulate; carbofuran is highly toxic to birds and was banned in the European Union.
1.4 Synthetic pyrethroids

Derived from natural pyrethrins of Chrysanthemum cinerariaefolium but with photostable structures: Type I (no alpha-cyano group): permethrin, allethrin, bifenthrin; Type II (alpha-cyano group): cypermethrin, deltamethrin, fenvalerate, lambda-cyhalothrin.

Mechanism: prolong the open state of voltage-gated sodium channels in insect nerve (Type I: repetitive firing and tremor, T-syndrome; Type II: persistent depolarisation, choreoathetosis and salivation, CS-syndrome); Type II also act on chloride channels.

Mammalian safety: rapidly hydrolysed by esterases and oxidised by cytochrome P450, poorly absorbed through skin, so acute mammalian toxicity is low (selectivity ratio insect to mammal about 1,000); the main human effect is paraesthesia of exposed skin; highly toxic to fish and bees. Piperonyl butoxide synergist inhibits insect P450.
1.5 Neonicotinoids and others (for completeness)
Imidacloprid, thiamethoxam, acetamiprid: agonists of insect nicotinic acetylcholine receptors; systemic in plants; implicated in bee decline; low mammalian toxicity.

Fungicides (mancozeb, carbendazim), herbicides (glyphosate, paraquat; paraquat has no antidote and causes pulmonary fibrosis) and fumigants (aluminium phosphide, phosphine, the commonest fatal poisoning in rural India; methyl bromide, phased out) are other residue classes with MRLs.
