blocks.text: 2. Toxicological Parameters: NOAEL, Safety Factor, ADI and MRL
2.1 Definitions

rows: The highest dose in a chronic animal study (usually the most sensitive species, two-year rat or dog study) at which no statistically or biologically significant adverse effect is observed; expressed in mg per kg body weight per day
Derived from toxicological studies submitted for registration
The lowest dose at which an adverse effect is seen; used with an extra factor when no NOAEL exists

Typically 100: a factor of 10 for extrapolation from animals to humans (interspecies) multiplied by 10 for variation among humans (intraspecies, children, elderly, sick); additional factors of 3 to 10 for severe effects, LOAEL-only data or database deficiencies
Convention of JMPR, JECFA and FSSAI
The amount of a chemical in food or drinking water that can be ingested daily over a lifetime without appreciable health risk, expressed in mg per kg body weight per day: ADI = NOAEL / safety factor
JMPR for pesticides, JECFA for additives, contaminants and veterinary drugs; in India, the Registration Committee under the Insecticides Act, 1968, and the FSSAI Scientific Panel
The amount that can be ingested in one meal or one day without appreciable risk; relevant for acutely toxic pesticides such as organophosphates and carbamates

The maximum concentration of a pesticide residue (mg/kg) legally permitted in or on a food commodity, derived from supervised field trials under Good Agricultural Practice (GAP: approved dose, number of applications, pre-harvest interval); it is a trading standard, not a toxicological threshold, and must be checked so that the Theoretical Maximum Daily Intake does not exceed the ADI

Codex Committee on Pesticide Residues internationally; in India, FSSAI under Regulation 2.3.1 of the Contaminants Regulations, based on recommendations of the Central Insecticides Board and Registration Committee
Provisional Tolerable Weekly or Monthly Intake, the equivalent of ADI for cumulative contaminants (lead, cadmium, mercury) that are not deliberately added
0.01 mg/kg for any pesticide on any commodity for which no MRL has been fixed (FSSAI, 2018 amendment), functioning as the limit of determination

blocks.text: 2.2 Worked derivation
Suppose the rat two-year NOAEL for a pesticide is 2.5 mg per kg body weight per day. ADI = 2.5 / 100 = 0.025 mg per kg per day. For a 60 kg adult, acceptable intake = 1.5 mg per day.

Suppose supervised trials under GAP on brinjal give highest residues of 0.4 mg/kg; the MRL is set at 0.5 mg/kg (rounded to the next standard level). If an Indian adult eats 100 g brinjal per day, the intake from brinjal at the MRL is 0.05 mg per day, which is 3.3 percent of the ADI; summing over all commodities on which the pesticide is registered gives the Theoretical Maximum Daily Intake, which must stay below the ADI or the GAP is revised.
2.3 The chain in one diagram

Animal toxicology ---> NOAEL ---> divide by safety factor (100) ---> ADI
                                                                       |
Field trials under GAP ---> residue data ---> MRL proposed              |
                                                 |                     |
                                                 v                     v
                              Dietary intake check: TMDI must be below ADI
                                                 |
                                                 v
                                   MRL notified by FSSAI (Reg 2.3.1)
2.4 Legal architecture in India

Insecticides Act, 1968 and Insecticides Rules, 1971: registration (Central Insecticides Board and Registration Committee), labelling (colour triangle: red for extremely toxic, yellow for highly toxic, blue for moderately toxic, green for slightly toxic), bans and restrictions.

Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, Section 19 and Section 20 read with the Contaminants Regulations: no insecticide may be used directly on food except fumigants registered for the purpose; MRLs in Regulation 2.3.1 (Table with over 200 pesticides and commodities); the 0.01 mg/kg default; the Monitoring of Pesticide Residues at National Level scheme (Ministry of Agriculture) generates the surveillance data.

A few representative MRLs (mg/kg; verify against the current table): DDT in milk and milk products 0.05 on a fat basis (older value 1.25 on fat), in fish 7.0 (older); HCH in milk 0.05 on fat; malathion in cereals 4.0, in vegetables 3.0; chlorpyrifos in cereals 0.05, in vegetables 0.2, in cottonseed 0.05; cypermethrin in vegetables 0.5; carbaryl in vegetables 5.0; carbofuran in vegetables 0.1.
3. Veterinary Drug Residues and Antibiotics
3.1 Why residues occur

Antibiotics are used in livestock, poultry, aquaculture and dairy for treatment, prophylaxis and (historically) growth promotion. Residues appear in milk, meat, eggs, honey and shrimp when the withdrawal period (time between the last dose and slaughter or milking) is not observed, when doses are excessive, or when prohibited drugs are used.
3.2 Classes, risks and limits

rows: Penicillin G, ampicillin, amoxicillin, cloxacillin, cephalosporins
Hypersensitivity and anaphylaxis in sensitised consumers at microgram doses; inhibition of dairy starter cultures (failed curd, cheese and yoghurt); resistance selection
Codex and FSSAI: benzylpenicillin in milk 4 micrograms per kg (0.004 mg/kg), in muscle 50 micrograms per kg
Discolouration of developing teeth and bone deposition in children, photosensitivity, resistance
FSSAI (Regulation 2.3.2): tetracycline and oxytetracycline 0.1 mg/kg in fish and shrimp; Codex: 100 micrograms per kg in muscle, 100 in milk, 600 in kidney
Hypersensitivity, thyroid tumours in rodents (sulphamethazine), resistance
Codex 100 micrograms per kg; FSSAI trimethoprim 0.05 mg/kg in seafood
Codex streptomycin 200 micrograms per kg in milk and muscle
Resistance transfer to human pathogens (Campylobacter, Salmonella); cartilage effects in young animals
Prohibited in aquaculture in India (shrimp export rejections); Codex MRLs for some species
Dose-independent, idiosyncratic aplastic anaemia (irreversible bone marrow failure, often fatal, with no threshold); grey baby syndrome; suspected carcinogen
Zero tolerance: prohibited in all food-producing animals (FSSAI, Codex, European Union, United States); minimum required performance limit of 0.3 micrograms per kg for detection
Furazolidone, nitrofurazone, furaltadone, nitrofurantoin (metabolites AOZ, SEM, AMOZ, AHD)
Zero tolerance; banned in aquaculture and livestock
DES and clenbuterol prohibited; India prohibits hormonal growth promoters in food animals
Used illegally as antifungal in fish farms; leucomalachite green residue

blocks.text: 3.3 Antimicrobial resistance: the mechanism of the public health threat

Sub-therapeutic antibiotic in feed or water
        |
        v
Selection pressure on gut and environmental bacteria of the animal
        |
        v
Survival and enrichment of resistant strains (chromosomal mutation or
acquisition of plasmid-borne resistance genes, transferred by conjugation)
        |
        v
Resistant Salmonella, Campylobacter, Escherichia coli and Enterococcus reach
humans through food, water, direct contact and manure on crops
        |
        v
Treatment failure in human infections; resistance genes transfer to human
pathogens (for example, colistin resistance gene mcr-1 from pigs to people)

Policy response: FSSAI Regulation 2.3.2 (2018) with a table of MRLs for about 103 antibiotics and pharmacologically active substances in meat, milk, eggs and aquaculture, plus an annexed list of substances prohibited for use in any food-producing animal (chloramphenicol, nitrofurans, nitroimidazoles, chlorpromazine, colchicine, dapsone, diethylstilbestrol, fluoroquinolones in aquaculture, glycopeptides, sulphonamides in shrimp, and others); the Coastal Aquaculture Authority list of 20 banned antibiotics for shrimp farming; National Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance (2017); Drugs and Cosmetics Rules amendment (2020) requiring withdrawal period on veterinary drug labels.
Analysis: screening by microbial inhibition tests (Delvotest, Charm) and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, confirmation by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry.

[HPSC EXAM TRAP] Chloramphenicol is not 'restricted to an MRL'; it is prohibited with zero tolerance because aplastic anaemia has no dose threshold. Penicillin residues matter at micrograms per kg because of allergy, not because of general toxicity. A pair claiming that 'cooking destroys all antibiotic residues' is false: tetracyclines and sulphonamides are partly heat-stable, and chloramphenicol survives boiling.
4. Process-Induced Chemical Contaminants
4.1 Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons (PAHs)

Chemistry: fused aromatic ring compounds formed by incomplete combustion and pyrolysis of organic matter above about 350 to 400 degrees Celsius. Benzo[a]pyrene (five rings) is the marker compound; the European Union 'PAH4' group adds benz[a]anthracene, benzo[b]fluoranthene and chrysene. Sixteen PAHs are prioritised by the United States Environmental Protection Agency.
Formation in food:

Charcoal grilling, barbecuing, tandoor: fat drips onto the fire, pyrolyses,
and PAH-laden smoke redeposits on the meat surface; direct flame contact
charring; higher with fattier meat, closer flame, longer time
        +
Smoking of fish, meat and cheese: wood smoke (hardwood above 400 degrees
Celsius) carries PAHs; traditional direct smoking far worse than liquid smoke
or indirect smoking with filtered smoke
        +
Drying of cereals, oilseeds and cocoa beans by direct combustion gases;
roasting of coffee; refined oils (coconut oil from copra dried over fires
is the classic high-PAH oil)
Mechanism of carcinogenesis:

Benzo[a]pyrene (inert procarcinogen)
        | cytochrome P450 1A1 and 1B1 (induced by PAHs themselves via the
        | aryl hydrocarbon receptor), then epoxide hydrolase, then P450 again
        v
Benzo[a]pyrene-7,8-dihydrodiol-9,10-epoxide (BPDE), the ultimate carcinogen
        |
        v
Covalent bulky adducts at the N2 position of guanine in DNA
        |
        v
If not repaired by nucleotide excision repair, replication across the adduct
causes G to T transversions; the characteristic mutation at codon 157 of the
TP53 tumour suppressor gene in smokers' lung cancer is the molecular signature
        |
        v
Initiation of carcinogenesis (Group 1 human carcinogen: lung, skin, bladder;
dietary association with gastrointestinal cancers)

Limits: European Union: benzo[a]pyrene 2 micrograms per kg and PAH4 12 micrograms per kg in smoked meat and fish (previously 5 micrograms per kg benzo[a]pyrene); 2 micrograms per kg benzo[a]pyrene and 10 PAH4 in oils and fats; 1 microgram per kg benzo[a]pyrene in infant foods. Codex has a code of practice for reducing PAH in smoking and drying. FSSAI has adopted benzo[a]pyrene ceilings in edible oils and smoked products in the harmonised amendments (verify the exact figures).

Mitigation: indirect smoking, filtered or liquid smoke, lower temperature, remove charred parts, marinate, pre-cook and finish briefly on the grill, keep food away from flames, avoid fat dripping, dry cereals with indirect heat.
Analysis: saponification or extraction, clean-up on silica or solid-phase extraction, high-performance liquid chromatography with fluorescence detection or gas chromatography-mass spectrometry.
4.2 Acrylamide
Discovery: Swedish National Food Administration, April 2002, after tunnel workers exposed to acrylamide grout were found to have no higher adduct levels than unexposed people who ate fried foods.
Formation:

Free asparagine (amino acid abundant in potato, wheat, rye, coffee beans)
        +
Reducing sugar carbonyl (glucose, fructose) 
        | Maillard reaction, above about 120 degrees Celsius, low moisture,
        | maximal 160 to 180 degrees Celsius
        v
Schiff base -> decarboxylated Amadori product (via Strecker-type chemistry)
        |
        v
Acrylamide (CH2=CH-CO-NH2): the carbon skeleton comes from asparagine,
the sugar carbonyl is the catalyst; minor routes from acrolein and acrylic acid

Foods: French fries and potato chips (highest, hundreds to thousands of micrograms per kg), biscuits, crispbread, breakfast cereals, roasted coffee (and coffee substitutes), toasted bread crust, roasted nuts; not formed in boiled or steamed foods (water keeps temperature at 100 degrees Celsius).

Toxicology: absorbed, distributed widely, metabolised by cytochrome P450 2E1 to glycidamide (an epoxide), which forms DNA adducts (N7-guanine); acrylamide itself binds sulphydryls and causes peripheral neuropathy (occupational), reproductive toxicity in rats; carcinogenic in rodents at multiple sites; Group 2A (probably carcinogenic to humans); haemoglobin adducts are the exposure biomarker.

Management: no legal maximum limits in most jurisdictions; European Union Regulation 2017/2158 sets benchmark levels (French fries 500 micrograms per kg, potato crisps 750, soft bread 50, breakfast cereals 150 to 300, roasted coffee 400, instant coffee 850) and mandatory mitigation measures; Codex Code of Practice (2009).

Mitigation: choose low-sugar potato varieties, store potatoes above 6 degrees Celsius (cold storage causes 'cold sweetening' and raises reducing sugars), blanch or soak cut potatoes (removes sugar and asparagine), add asparaginase enzyme to dough, lower frying temperature (below 175 degrees Celsius), fry to golden yellow not brown, add calcium or citric acid, shorter roasting of coffee.
Analysis: liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry or gas chromatography-mass spectrometry after bromination; isotope dilution with carbon-13 labelled acrylamide.
4.3 Ethyl Carbamate (Urethane)

Chemistry: NH2-CO-O-C2H5, the ethyl ester of carbamic acid; a natural trace constituent of all fermented foods and beverages; once used as a medicine and as a co-solvent, banned when found carcinogenic in 1943.
Formation routes:

Route 1 (wine, sake, yoghurt, bread, soy sauce): yeast metabolises arginine
(arginase) releasing urea; urea + ethanol -> ethyl carbamate + ammonia,
accelerated by heat and storage time; citrulline from lactic acid bacteria
(arginine deiminase pathway) is a second precursor via carbamyl phosphate

Route 2 (stone-fruit spirits: kirsch, slivovitz, apricot and plum brandies):
cyanogenic glycosides in pits release hydrogen cyanide; cyanide is oxidised
(copper and light catalysed) to cyanate; cyanate + ethanol -> ethyl carbamate;
this is why distilled stone-fruit spirits have the highest levels

Route 3: diethyl pyrocarbonate (a former wine preservative) + ammonia ->
ethyl carbamate; the preservative was banned in 1972 for this reason

Toxicology: metabolised by cytochrome P450 2E1 to vinyl carbamate and its epoxide, which forms DNA adducts; multisite carcinogen in rodents (lung, liver, lymphoma, mammary); Group 2A (probably carcinogenic to humans); JECFA margin of exposure for heavy consumers of stone-fruit spirits is of concern.
Typical levels: wines 1 to 30 micrograms per L; sake and sherry higher; stone-fruit brandies up to several mg per L; bread and yoghurt a few micrograms per kg.

Limits: Canada (the first regulator, 1985): table wine 30 micrograms per L, fortified wine 100, distilled spirits 150, fruit brandies 400, sake 200; United States voluntary targets (wine 15 micrograms per L); Codex Code of Practice (2011) for stone-fruit distillates; European Union target 1 mg per L in stone-fruit spirits.

Mitigation: low-urea yeast strains, acid urease addition to wine and sake, limiting arginine (vineyard nitrogen management), removing pits before mashing, copper catalysts in stills to remove cyanide, storing spirits in the dark, controlled distillation cuts.
Analysis: extraction, gas chromatography-mass spectrometry with selected ion monitoring; deuterated internal standard.

Grilled meat, smoked fish, coconut oil, roasted coffee
EU 2 micrograms per kg in smoked meat and fish
Maillard above 120 degrees Celsius, low moisture
EU benchmark 500 micrograms per kg fries
Urea or citrulline or cyanate plus ethanol
Canada 30 micrograms per L wine, 400 fruit brandy
Oil refining deodorisation above 200 degrees Celsius

blocks.text: 4. Dedicated [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Compendium
Trap 1: Neurolathyrism (BOAA, Lathyrus sativus, spastic paraparesis) versus osteolathyrism (beta-aminopropionitrile, Lathyrus odoratus, skeletal collagen defect).

Trap 2: Linamarin is cassava; amygdalin is bitter almond and apricot kernel; dhurrin is sorghum. Boiling intact bitter cassava is less effective than grating followed by soaking because heat inactivates linamarase before it can free the cyanide.
Trap 3: Favism affects only G6PD-deficient individuals; the glycosides are heat-stable; the mechanism is oxidative haemolysis, not cyanide and not allergy.
Trap 4: Slow cooking of kidney beans at 70 to 80 degrees Celsius increases lectin activity up to five-fold; only boiling destroys it.
Trap 5: Kunitz inhibitor is single-headed (trypsin) and heat-labile; Bowman-Birk is double-headed (trypsin and chymotrypsin) and heat-stable.
Trap 6: Glycoalkaloid limit 200 mg/kg is for the total of solanine plus chaconine; they survive boiling and frying; peeling is the remedy.

Trap 7: Goitrin (from progoitrin) blocks thyroid peroxidase and is not overcome by iodine; thiocyanate (from indole and other glucosinolates, and from cassava) blocks the iodide symporter and is overcome by iodine. Sinigrin gives allyl isothiocyanate, not goitrin.

Trap 8: Argemone: nitric acid test is the screening test (0.25 percent); paper chromatography is the confirmatory, most sensitive test (0.0001 percent); the alkaloid is sanguinarine; the statutory tolerance is nil.

Trap 9: ASP is from a diatom (Pseudo-nitzschia); PSP, DSP and NSP are from dinoflagellates. Saxitoxin and tetrodotoxin block sodium channels; brevetoxin and ciguatoxin activate them; okadaic acid inhibits phosphatases, not channels.
Trap 10: Scombroid poisoning is not an allergy, is not destroyed by cooking or canning, and is prevented by rapid chilling below 4 degrees Celsius after catch.

Trap 11: Lead inhibits ALAD and ferrochelatase (anaemia with normal iron), cadmium causes Itai-itai (Toyama, Japan), methylmercury causes Minamata (Kumamoto, Japan), arsenic causes blackfoot disease (Taiwan) and arsenicosis (West Bengal). Do not cross-match the place names.
Trap 12: ADI = NOAEL / 100 (not multiplied). MRL is a Good Agricultural Practice trading standard, not a toxicological threshold; the default MRL where none exists is 0.01 mg/kg.

Trap 13: Carbamate acetylcholinesterase inhibition is reversible without ageing; pralidoxime is for organophosphates. Chloramphenicol has zero tolerance (aplastic anaemia has no threshold); penicillin's milk MRL is 4 micrograms per kg because of allergy.

Trap 14: Acrylamide needs asparagine plus reducing sugar above 120 degrees Celsius and is absent from boiled food; benzo[a]pyrene comes from pyrolysis above 350 to 400 degrees Celsius and smoke; ethyl carbamate comes from urea or cyanate plus ethanol in fermented and distilled products.
5. Stage 1 Revision Bank: Count-Based Pair Questions (exactly 4)

Instruction: For each question, three statements are given. Determine how many are correct and choose Only 1 / Only 2 / All 3 / None. Verification uses N = c1 + c2 + c3, where c = 1 for a correct pair and c = 0 for an incorrect pair.
Question 1: Legume toxicants
(i) BOAA, the neurotoxin of Lathyrus sativus, acts as an agonist at AMPA-type glutamate receptors.
(ii) Amygdalin is the principal cyanogenic glycoside of cassava (tapioca).
(iii) The Kunitz inhibitor of soybean inhibits chymotrypsin more strongly than trypsin.
Step-by-step verification:
(i): BOAA is a glutamate analogue and AMPA receptor agonist causing excitotoxic degeneration of corticospinal tracts. Correct. c1 = 1.
(ii): The cassava glycoside is linamarin (with minor lotaustralin); amygdalin is in bitter almond and apricot kernels. Incorrect. c2 = 0.
(iii): Kunitz inhibitor is single-headed and inhibits trypsin primarily; chymotrypsin inhibition is a feature of the double-headed Bowman-Birk inhibitor. Incorrect. c3 = 0.
Answer: Only 1.
Question 2: Marine biotoxins
(i) Saxitoxin causes paralysis by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels at the neuromuscular junction.
(ii) Domoic acid, the amnesic shellfish poison, is produced by the dinoflagellate Alexandrium.
(iii) Brevetoxins of Karenia brevis act by activating (opening) voltage-gated sodium channels.
Step-by-step verification:
(i): Saxitoxin plugs site 1 of the sodium channel; nerve conduction fails; respiratory paralysis follows. Correct. c1 = 1.
(ii): Domoic acid is produced by the diatom Pseudo-nitzschia, not by a dinoflagellate; Alexandrium produces saxitoxin. Incorrect. c2 = 0.
(iii): Brevetoxins bind site 5 and keep the channel open, causing persistent depolarisation. Correct. c3 = 1.
Answer: Only 2.
Question 3: Heavy metals
(i) Lead causes anaemia by inhibiting delta-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase and ferrochelatase.
(ii) Itai-itai disease of the Jinzu River basin in Japan was caused by chronic cadmium exposure through rice.
(iii) The statutory ceiling for tin in canned foods is 250 mg/kg.
Step-by-step verification:
(i): Lead displaces zinc from ALAD and inhibits ferrochelatase, blocking haem synthesis; zinc protoporphyrin accumulates. Correct. c1 = 1.
(ii): Cadmium from the Kamioka mine contaminated irrigation water and rice, causing renal tubular damage and osteomalacia. Correct. c2 = 1.
(iii): FSSAI, in line with Codex, sets 250 mg/kg for canned foods (150 mg/kg for canned beverages). Correct. c3 = 1.
Answer: All 3.
Question 4: Residues and toxicological parameters
(i) Carbamate insecticides cause irreversible 'ageing' of phosphorylated acetylcholinesterase, so pralidoxime is essential in their treatment.
(ii) Chloramphenicol has a defined Maximum Residue Limit in milk under the FSSAI Contaminants Regulations.
(iii) The Acceptable Daily Intake is obtained by multiplying the NOAEL by the safety factor of 100.
Step-by-step verification:
(i): Carbamates carbamylate the enzyme reversibly; the bond hydrolyses spontaneously; there is no ageing; pralidoxime is not routinely indicated. Incorrect. c1 = 0.
(ii): Chloramphenicol is on the prohibited (zero-tolerance) list for all food-producing animals because aplastic anaemia has no threshold; no MRL exists. Incorrect. c2 = 0.
(iii): ADI = NOAEL divided by the safety factor (NOAEL / 100), not multiplied. Incorrect. c3 = 0.
Answer: None.
6. Stage 2 Model Answer (10 Marks)
Question: Detail the biochemical etiology, clinical symptoms, and processing detoxification methods for Neurolathyrism and Epidemic Dropsy.
Introduction (1 mark)

Neurolathyrism and epidemic dropsy are the two classical Indian food toxicoses of plant origin: the first arises from an inherent neurotoxic amino acid in a legume consumed as a famine staple; the second arises from adulteration of mustard oil with the seed oil of a weed. Both are entirely preventable by processing or regulatory control, and both remain statutory concerns under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
Part A: Neurolathyrism (4.5 marks)

Etiology. Khesari dal (Lathyrus sativus) contains 0.1 to 2.5 percent of beta-N-oxalyl-L-alpha,beta-diaminopropionic acid (BOAA or ODAP), a water-soluble non-protein amino acid in which oxalic acid is amide-linked to the beta-amino group of diaminopropionic acid. BOAA is a structural analogue of glutamate and acts as an agonist at AMPA-type ionotropic glutamate receptors on motor neurons. Sustained receptor activation causes sodium and calcium influx (excitotoxicity), inhibition of mitochondrial complex I, oxidative stress and glutathione depletion, leading to selective degeneration of Betz cells and the long corticospinal axons to the lower limbs. Disease follows consumption of khesari as more than about 30 percent of the diet for 2 to 6 months, mainly in young men doing hard labour, and is aggravated by deficiency of sulphur amino acids and zinc.

Clinical features. Prodromal calf cramps and heaviness of the legs are followed by a spastic gait with scissoring and toe-walking. The disease is staged as no-stick, one-stick, two-stick and crawler stages. Examination shows hypertonia, exaggerated knee and ankle reflexes, clonus and an extensor plantar response, with sensation, sphincters and intellect spared. The paraparesis is permanent; there is no antidote.

Detoxification. Because BOAA is water-soluble, every effective method is a wet method with discarding of the soak water: (1) steeping dehusked dal in hot water at 60 to 70 degrees Celsius for one hour removes 70 to 80 percent; (2) parboiling (soaking, boiling or steaming, discarding water, sun-drying) removes 80 to 90 percent; (3) soaking in 1 to 2 percent lime water (calcium hydroxide) hydrolyses the oxalyl amide bond and removes up to 90 percent; (4) lactic fermentation gives partial removal. Dry roasting and frying are ineffective. Low-toxin cultivars (ODAP below 0.1 percent) are a breeding solution. Statutorily, the sale of kesari gram, kesari dal, kesari flour and their admixtures is prohibited under the Food Safety and Standards (Prohibition and Restrictions on Sales) Regulations, 2011 (continuing Rule 44A of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules).
Part B: Epidemic Dropsy (4 marks)

Etiology. Seeds of Argemone mexicana (prickly poppy, satyanashi), a mustard-field weed, resemble mustard seeds and contaminate or are deliberately added to mustard oil. Argemone oil contains the benzophenanthridine alkaloids sanguinarine (about 0.3 percent) and dihydrosanguinarine (about 1 percent), the latter converted to sanguinarine in the body. Sanguinarine inhibits Na+/K+-ATPase in vascular endothelium and cardiac muscle, increases capillary permeability, dilates capillaries, inhibits pyruvate oxidation and glucose-6-phosphatase, and causes oxidative stress. The result is plasma leakage into tissues, pooling of blood and high-output cardiac strain. Oil with about 1 percent argemone oil is sufficient to cause disease.

Clinical features. Whole families fall ill 1 to 3 weeks after consuming the oil. After a gastrointestinal prodrome there is bilateral, pitting, non-inflammatory oedema of the legs with erythema and tenderness, dilated veins and skin nodules; tachycardia, cardiomegaly and congestive heart failure (the main cause of death, about 5 percent); and raised intra-ocular pressure causing glaucoma, with retinal haemorrhages and possible blindness. Anaemia, fever, hepatomegaly and proteinuria also occur. The Delhi outbreak of 1998 (about 3,000 cases and more than 60 deaths) led to the restriction on sale of loose edible oils.

Detection and control. There is no detoxification; the control is prevention of adulteration, supported by analysis: the nitric acid test (5 mL oil shaken with 5 mL concentrated nitric acid gives a red to orange-red colour; sensitivity about 0.25 percent), the ferric chloride test (orange-brown precipitate on heating; about 1 percent), and the confirmatory paper chromatography of the alcoholic extract, in which sanguinarine fluoresces orange-yellow under ultraviolet light and is detectable to 0.0001 percent; thin-layer and high-performance liquid chromatography quantify the alkaloids. The standard for all edible oils requires the argemone test to be negative (nil tolerance), and adulteration causing injury is punishable under Section 59 of the Act.
Conclusion (0.5 mark)

Neurolathyrism is an inherent-toxicant problem solved by wet processing and sale prohibition; epidemic dropsy is an adulteration problem solved by analytical surveillance and packaged-oil regulation. The Food Safety Officer's role is to enforce both: seize khesari admixtures in the dal trade and sample mustard oil for the argemone test.
18. Stage 2 Model Answer: 15 Marks
Question
Examine the classification, physiological mechanisms and statutory regulatory framework governing heavy metals and agrochemical residues in food.
Model answer

Heavy metals and agrochemical residues are chemical hazards that may enter food through soil, water, industrial activity, agricultural practices, veterinary treatment, processing equipment and environmental deposition. Their risk depends on chemical form, dose, duration, bioavailability and consumer susceptibility.
Classification
Important toxic elements include lead, cadmium, mercury, arsenic and tin.
Lead is a neurotoxic and haematotoxic metal.
Cadmium is a cumulative renal and skeletal toxicant.
Mercury exists as elemental, inorganic and methylmercury forms.
Arsenic occurs as trivalent, pentavalent and organic compounds; inorganic arsenic is the major food-safety concern.
Tin may leach from food cans, particularly into acidic foods.

Agrochemical residues include organochlorine pesticides, organophosphates, carbamates and synthetic pyrethroids. Veterinary residues include beta-lactams, tetracyclines, sulfonamides and prohibited substances such as chloramphenicol.
Physiological mechanisms
Lead

Lead inhibits delta-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase and ferrochelatase, thereby impairing haem synthesis and causing anaemia. It also disrupts calcium signalling and neurotransmitter function. Children may suffer impaired cognition, developmental delay and behavioural changes.
Cadmium

Cadmium induces metallothionein and accumulates in proximal renal tubules. Chronic exposure produces tubular proteinuria, reduced renal function, bone demineralisation and osteomalacia. Severe chronic exposure is associated with Itai-Itai disease.
Mercury

Methylmercury is absorbed efficiently from fish, crosses the blood–brain and placental barriers and causes neurological and developmental toxicity. Bioaccumulation and biomagnification make large predatory fish important exposure sources. Minamata disease is the classical example.
Arsenic

Trivalent arsenic binds sulfhydryl groups and inhibits enzymes. Pentavalent arsenic can interfere with phosphate-dependent metabolism. Chronic exposure causes skin lesions, neuropathy, vascular disease and cancer. Contaminated groundwater and rice are important exposure pathways in affected areas.
Tin
Inorganic tin leached from cans may cause gastrointestinal irritation, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea at high concentrations.
Organophosphate pesticides

Organophosphates phosphorylate acetylcholinesterase and cause accumulation of acetylcholine. Muscarinic, nicotinic and central nervous system symptoms may occur, including salivation, bronchospasm, fasciculations, convulsions and respiratory failure.
Carbamates
Carbamates reversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase and produce a similar but generally shorter-lived cholinergic syndrome.
Organochlorines
Organochlorines are persistent, lipophilic and bioaccumulative. They may cause neurotoxicity, endocrine effects, reproductive effects and chronic organ toxicity.
Synthetic pyrethroids
Pyrethroids prolong sodium-channel opening and may cause paraesthesia, tremor and seizures in severe exposure.
Veterinary drugs
Residues can cause allergy, direct toxicity, disruption of gut flora, antimicrobial resistance and treatment failure. Chloramphenicol is prohibited because of the risk of aplastic anaemia.
Regulatory framework

The statutory framework is based on the Food Safety and Standards legislation and the applicable regulations relating to contaminants, toxins and residues. Maximum limits for heavy metals are generally commodity-specific. Separate standards may apply to milk, cereals, pulses, vegetables, spices, meat, fish, canned foods and rice. Therefore, a universal lead, cadmium, mercury or arsenic limit should not be quoted without identifying the food category.

Tin has a commonly examined statutory ceiling of 250 milligrams per kilogram in canned food. For arsenic, the distinction between total arsenic and inorganic arsenic is essential. Fish standards may distinguish total mercury from methylmercury or apply species-specific controls.

Pesticide maximum residue limits are individual pesticide–commodity combinations. A residue below the maximum residue limit is legally acceptable for that combination, whereas the acceptable daily intake is a health-based exposure estimate for the consumer. The no observed adverse effect level is used in risk assessment, and a safety factor accounts for uncertainty and biological variability.

Veterinary drugs are regulated through permitted residue limits, withdrawal periods and prohibitions. Chloramphenicol is treated as a prohibited residue and is not governed by an ordinary positive tolerance level.
Monitoring and enforcement
Food control requires:
Risk-based sampling
Representative collection
Validated extraction
Atomic absorption or inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry for metals
Gas chromatography or liquid chromatography coupled with tandem mass spectrometry for pesticide and veterinary residues
Screening followed by confirmatory testing
Calibration, recovery and uncertainty assessment
Comparison with the current notified legal limit
Traceability and recall when violations are confirmed
Conclusion

Heavy metals cause toxicity through enzyme inhibition, oxidative stress, renal accumulation, neurotoxicity and interference with mineral or haem metabolism. Agrochemical residues cause acute cholinergic toxicity, chronic neurological or endocrine effects and antimicrobial resistance. Effective regulation requires commodity-specific maximum limits, scientifically derived acceptable daily intakes, withdrawal periods, prohibition of dangerous substances and reliable laboratory surveillance.
